#4507. Young sea turtles make an unexpected home in the Gulf of Oman

Published Nov 13, 2026 12:00 AM EST

For one group of young sea turtles, a protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) proved a perfect oasis. A team tracking nine juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) found they were spending over 80 percent of their time in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area, a human-made lagoon on the UAE’s Gulf of Oman coast. Large numbers of turtles are also found in this basin built beyond the salt-tolerant trees and shrubs along the coast. A study published today in the journal Aquatic Conservation details the findings.

In 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees. The resulting Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area has been recognized as a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention and as a Key Biodiversity Area since 2013.

“Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr. Owen Exeter, a study co-author and marine conservation ecologist from the University of Exeter, said in a statement. “The fact these turtles are using the artificial basin appears to be a happy accident, and an example of how wildlife can find a way in a world increasingly shaped by humans. However, without the natural mangroves connecting to this system, it’s unlikely that this would have occurred.

According to the team, the floor of the basin is covered with algae, which likely means the turtles have enough food. A few sharks are making their way to this habitat.

The turtles are now also showing “strong reliance” in the man-made basin, with five times higher odds of being found there than in surrounding habitats.

While this spot can be a refuge, the natural mangrove channels also play a critical role in connecting the juvenile turtles (those with a shell less than 23 inches across) to the sea. These channels allow them to move with the tides and show the importance of protecting the entire ecosystem, not just parts of it.

“The government of Sharjah currently protects most of this area from building development, fishing and boating—preserving the last mangrove ecosystem on UAE’s east coast,” Exeter said. “Coastal wetlands are tropical nature hotspots, providing essential nursery and foraging habitats for species including sea turtles. Wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems globally, so we urgently need to understand how key species use both modified and protected wetlands.”

While these findings are positive for the turtles living in the protected area, their life cycle depends on nesting beaches. Many of these beaches have already been lost to coastal development, and fishing, vessel traffic, and pollution affect the other nearby areas.

One of the turtles swam over 430 miles south to central Oman, highlighting the need for conservation management of these mobile species once they are old enough to leave critical wetland sites.

“Overall, our findings show that coastal wetlands, including engineered ones, can provide valuable habitat for juvenile turtles, provided they are designed for ecological connectivity and subsequent human pressures and threats are minimised,” concluded study co-author Brendan Whittington-Jones from the Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA) who led the study.

#4506. The new BMW i3 just proved how efficient an EV can be after a nearly 3,700-mile road trip

Who says long EV road trips mean hours at charging stations? BMW drove the new i3 for over 3 days, covering nearly 3,700 miles, and it took less than 3 hours of charging.

BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.

The Paneurpeana, as it’s called, is considered the benchmark for range and charging speed. The route begins at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe you can reach by car, and ends in Tarifa, Spain, the southernmost point of mainland Europe.

BMW drove the new i3 50 xDrive for a total of 3,658 miles (5,886.7 km) across eight countries and spent just 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds charging at an average of 275 kW.

The performance beat the previous record by more than seven hours, according to Mike Reichelt, head of BMW’s Neue Klasse

BMW said the charging points were not predetermined and that it had to account for external factors such as weather and traffic jams.

The new i3 was impressively efficient during the trip, consuming an average of just 12.5 kWh per 100 km, beating its official WLTP combined energy consumption of 18-13.4 kWh/100 km.

BMW said the trip took 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes, with an average speed of 79.7 km/h, and that the i3 was charged exclusively at public charging points across national charging networks.

The vehicle was driven at all times by a single driver and was not modified in any way, in terms of hardware or software, from the standard i3 available for purchase.

BMW’s new i3 uses a 108.7 kWh battery and Gen6 eDrive system that provides a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

With a drag coefficient of just 0.21, the new i3 is the most aerodynamically efficient BMW vehicle to date.

In the US, BMW said the new 2027 i3 50 xDrive will offer an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 468 miles.

With an 800V architecture, the electric sedan can add nearly 262 miles (423 km) of range (WLTP) in about 10 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds up to 400 kW. In the US, the i3 has a built-in NACS port.

Very reasonable. I've been with NK iX3 from Spain to Estonia and the experience is real - low consumption, great comfort and really fast charging. And there are more and more high speed chargers every month.

Like the new iX3, the i3 features BMW’s Neue Klasse interior design. The setup consists of BMW’s massive 43″ Panoramic Vision display that spans the base of the windshield and a 17.9″ floating central infotainment display.

The new BMW i3 50 xDrive is on sale in Germany starting at €65,900 with a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

In the US, the 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive and 2027 iX3 50 xDrive are available to order, both starting at $61,500.

#4505. A Tesla Aftermarket Shop Wants to Build the Cybertruck Under License

Unplugged Performance took to Tesla boss Elon Musk’s preferred social medium of choice, X, to make the offer.

The Tesla Cybertruck, as you may well have heard by now, is on death row. How the news hits you will likely depend on what your opinions on the truck that company CEO “Technoking” Elon Musk once described as “what Bladerunner would have driven.” Those who dislike the steel-bodied machine range from pleased to gloating; fans, meanwhile, are rending garments and clutching their vowel-less vanity plates. Alas, poor Cybertruck; I knew him, Elon!

But one group of Tesla enthusiasts are aiming to take matters into their own hands. Unplugged Performance, an aftermarket shop specializing in Teslas, has taken to social media to entreat the automaker not to kill off the slab-sided pickup, but rather, to license its production out to them instead.

The company took to X—which is owned by Musk, who is also, shall we say, a vocal user—to make the offer. “An open offer to Tesla: We fully support putting Cybercab first, and we’d be glad to take the Cybertruck line off your hands. We’d fund it with a consortium of investors and run it at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus,” Unplugged Performance wrote.

That offer, unsurprisingly, evoked a reaction amongst Internet-active fans of the Cybertruck, as well as quite a few questions for specifics. To their credit, Unplugged Performance responded with a comprehensive amount of detail regarding the plan so far. “A fair question we’re hearing: can UP really run the Cybertruck vehicle line? Not alone, and not overnight,” the brand tweeted (X-ed?), before elaborating that it intends to round up investors and manufacturing partners in the months leading up to Tesla’s planned changeover of its Texas plant that will use the capacity currently occupied by the truck to build autonomous Cybercabs.

“We believe this is highly fundable because one production platform serves three markets: existing demand for the pickup, pent-up demand for a seven-seat SUV, and Robotaxi network vehicles in useful all-terrain form factors (seven-seat people movers, cargo haulers, and pickups),” Unplugged Performance continued.

“Should add,” the shop added, “the number of Tesla alumni who have reached out offering to help has been overwhelming. For anyone questioning talent or experience, we already have a strong and resourceful team, and many people who helped build these vehicles want to participate and see the platform live on.”

As of this story’s Wednesday afternoon publication, Tesla and Musk don’t appear to have offered a public response to Unplugged’s offer. That said, Musk did post on Wednesday that pickup production is being extended through summer of next year to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” And given his follow-up, who knows? Maybe he’d be open to letting someone else take over after that.

Will Sabel Courtney is a contributing editor at Road & Track. #4504. Smartwatch blood pressure monitoring was okay. AI is making it better.

Published Nov 13, 2026 9:39 AM EST

When the United States Food and Drug Administration cleared the Apple Watch’s Hypertension Notification Feature last year, some saw it as a turning point in the fight against one of the leading causes of cardiac disease. Rather than booking a doctor’s appointment and strapping a bulging cuff around one’s arm, users could instead receive passive hypertension alerts from the watch’s optical sensors to track blood flow patterns. Watch wearers who were previously unaware that they had signs of this ever-common “silent killer” would receive an alert advising them to seek out a clinician.  Early intervention could mean a better chance at beginning life-saving interventions.

While that sounds great, the reality of smartwatch hypertension tools is more nuanced. Apple’s own validation data showed that their feature would miss around 59 percent of people with undiagnosed high blood pressure. Newer United States population level research from the University of Utah and the University of Pennsylvania went a step further, and warned that the absence of an alert could give wearers a false sense of security, potentially making them less likely to go get a proper cuff screening. The feature, in other words, isn’t necessarily harmful, but it also isn’t a medical silver bullet.

That context is worth keeping in mind when considering new research from scientists at Google and a clinical partner from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recently published in the journal Nature. The team claims they created a new AI system that pairs with a consumer smartwatch to passively detect signs of high blood pressure, “with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed blood pressure devices.”

The new system draws on two sensors already found in many consumer smartwatches: an optical pulse sensor (which tracks changes in blood volume at the wrist) and an accelerometer. An AI algorithm then analyzes several days of  readings, factors in the wearer’s height, and then calculates the probability that they have hypertension.

Google’s system builds on Apple’s approach by adding in the watch’s accelerometer to the mix, which can pick up the faint wrist vibrations of each heartbeat. The results look promising. In initial screenings, the combined system caught more cases of high blood pressure than a standard office cuff reading, though it still missed about a third of cases. And while the researchers involved still advise against using the tool as a substitute for seeing a doctor, it’s potentially another step forward in attempts to use common wearable tech to catch underlying signs of disease earlier.

“By gently prompting at-risk individuals to step into a clinic for formal assessment, this technology holds the potential to significantly close the global awareness gap and catch hypertension before it causes permanent cardiovascular damage,” Google researchers note in a blog post.

Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the U.S. , claiming more than  900,000 lives in 2023 alone. Chronic high blood pressure (referred to as hypertension medically) is one of the key early risk factors. Around half of all Americans likely have it, but an estimated four in ten people don’t know they have it, partly because it often does not present with any clear symptoms. And while hypertension is treatable when caught early, many simply don’t see a doctor often enough to be screened regularly. That combination of an invisible condition and spotty screening makes the issue an attractive target for always-on smartwatch sensors.

The sensors on commercial smartwatches can pick up useful data, but those signals still need to be interpreted by an AI model. In this case, Google says it trained its system on nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data collected from 2,109 people. The optical sensor captures the shapes of each pulse wave at the wrist, while the accelerometer shows signs of the subtle physical vibrations that occur at the wrist when blood is ejected from the heart into the aorta. Both of those signal data are cut into 5-second PPG and ACC waveforms. The AI converts those signal snippets into numerical summaries, which Google refers to as an “embedding.”

Over time, the AI model was able to pore over those different numerical values and determine which types of pulses are likely associated with hypertension. By analyzing data collected from one wearer to the next, the AI sees numerical patterns that distinguish one person’s signals from another. But simply relying on a measurement from one point in time risks introducing what the researcher calls “environmental noise” that can skew results. To account for all that noise, they aggregated the sensors’ data over multiple days of use to establish a wearer’s persistent state. That data then gets fed into a logistic regression classifier, which comes out with a score corresponding to a person’s likelihood of having hypertension.

The team tested their system on 196 participants over seven days of real-world monitoring, checking their results against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, which they refer to as the “gold standard” in the field. The AI smartwatch system ultimately detected hypertension with a sensitivity of 65.8 percent. That means 65.8 percent of people who were proven to have hypertension were accurately identified by their AI system. That’s far from perfect, but it was still higher than the 55.3 percent caught by initial office cuff readings in the study.

“Taken together, the results show that our system can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed BP devices in the existing clinical framework,” Google notes.

Like Apple before it, Google and the other medical researchers involved in this story were quick to stress that these findings, noteworthy as they may sound, shouldn’t lead people to think of this system as a complete replacement for clinical blood pressure monitoring .Going to see actual human doctors isn’t going away anytime soon, but this system, if widely accessible, could help nudge more people towards getting checked out.

#4502. What is Gonzo? We asked three biologists.

Published Nov 13, 2026 9:39 AM EST

Many of the Muppets are pretty easy to pin down, species-wise. Kermit is a frog. Fozzie is a bear. Miss Piggy is, obviously, a feisty piggy. But Gonzo—with his blue-ish fur, bulging eyes, tuft of purple feathers, and long, curved nose that looks a little like a beak—is something of an enigma. The writers of the Muppets have avoided the question of what Gonzo is for years.

Well, in a new episode of Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast, we asked three biologists to break down exactly what Gonzo is. We also talk to Muppets legend and Gonzo performer Dave Goelz to get his take.

Ask Us Anything answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions—from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask. So, yes, there’s a reason candy tastes different now and no, you don’t need to worry about Yellowstone’s supervolcano blowing up anytime soon. If you have a question for us, send us a note. Nothing is too silly or simple.

This episode is based on the Popular Science article “What kind of animal is Gonzo?”

Listen and follow Ask Us Anything on your favorite podcast platform:

Spotify | Apple Podcasts | YouTube | Or wherever you get your podcasts.

Sarah Durn: Picture some of the most recognizable characters from The Muppets. Maybe you’re thinking of Kermit the Frog, or Miss Piggy, or Fozzie Bear. But today, we’re talking about a Muppet who’s a little harder to describe: Gonzo. You know the one. He’s got bluish fur, big bulging eyes, a tuft of purple feathers on his head, and a long curved nose that looks a little like a beak.

You might know him as The Great Gonzo, the fearless daredevil, performance artist, and stunt Muppet who eats tires, catches cannonballs bare-handed, and courts his beloved Camilla, who is a chicken. So yeah, Gonzo is a pretty unusual guy. But here’s something you might never have stopped to think about. What exactly is Gonzo?

Is he a bird, a lizard, an alien? All of the above? For decades, Muppets cast and creators have mostly dodged the question when asked, but here at Popular Science, we wanted a more scientific answer. So we asked three biologists to take a closer look at Gonzo’s anatomy and tell us what kind of creature he might be.

Their answers took us somewhere we definitely weren’t expecting, all the way back to the age of the dinosaurs. So what is Gonzo, and can science finally solve one of the Muppets’ greatest mysteries?

Welcome to Ask Us Anything from the editors of Popular Science, where we answer your questions about our weird world. From “does candy taste different now?” to “how do airplane toilets work?” No question is too simple or too out there. I’m Sarah Durn, an editor at Popular Science.

Annie Colbert: And hello, I am Popular Science editor-in-chief and huge Muppets fan, Annie Colbert

SD: Here at PopSci, we’re always pondering weirdo questions.

AC: And this week we’re wondering: What animal might Gonzo be? Is he an animal at all?

SD: It’s a very fair question, one the writers of the Muppets have spent over 50 years dodging. In one film, Gonzo even asked to be called a whatever.

AC: Which is pretty classic Gonzo, but as science journalists, “whatever” doesn’t quite hold up under peer review.

SD: Not at all. So we took Gonzo’s anatomy to actual evolutionary biologists and paleontologists to see if they could decode his unique physiology.

AC: Let me guess. They told you he’s just a funny-looking bird?

SD: That’s what you might think. He’s got that down curved beak thing, a floof atop on his head that kinda looks like feathers, and a chicken for a girlfriend.

But when you look at the clues, like his three unfused fingers and fuzzy skin, things get way weirder.

AC: Weirder than a blue guy who eats rubber tires and catches cannonballs?

SD: Well, at least on a similar level of weird, I guess. Some scientists think his traits point tens of millions of years into the past, past modern birds, straight into the age of carnivorous dinosaurs.

AC: Wait, are you telling me that Gonzo might be closer to a T-Rex than a turkey?

SD: Let’s just say Jurassic Park might need a Muppets section.

AC: Hmm. Now, before we try to decode the Muppet fossil record, we wanna know, what questions are nagging you? If there’s something you’ve always wanted to know, submit your questions by clicking the Ask Us link at popsci.com/ask.

Again, that’s popsci.com/ask, and click the Ask Us link.

AC: We’ll be right back after this quick break to find out if science can really classify the greatest daredevil in puppet history.

SD: And stick around to the end, because we’ll be joined by the legendary David Goelz, the original and longtime performer of Gonzo, to hear his take on what sort of life form Gonzo might be.

And we’re back. Now, Annie, before we dive into the mysteries of Muppet evolution, we need to establish your credentials here a bit, because you are far from just a casual fan. You are a certified Muppet expert.

SD: Okay, so how did your Muppet obsession begin?

AC: You know, there’s no start to my love of Muppets.

I grew up in a Muppet house with The Muppet Show and Sesame Street always on. I’ve always identified as a bit of a whimsical weirdo. I dressed up even as Grundgetta, who is Oscar the Grouch’s girlfriend, for Halloween in fourth grade. No one knew who I was, but I will share a photo, so you can judge for yourselves, listeners.

And I would say generally if people know one or two things about me, it’s either that I have strange cats or that I love the Muppets. It’s a very big part of who I am.

SD: I mean, you have your own Muppet wiki page.

AC: I do! It just appeared one day after I did some fun work with Sesame Street, but it is a life highlight to have.

SD: I mean, so casual, so cool. Um, honestly, I think I’m a little intimidated because I am walking into this episode possessing maybe 1% of your Muppet knowledge. I think I saw a couple of the Muppet films when I was growing up.

AC: Don’t worry at all. The Muppets accept all, even the uninitiated.

SD: Well, I’m very happy to be here as an uninitiated Muppet fan, especially because this episode is just so fun and goofy and feels very PopSci.

AC: Yes, absolutely. I love giving scientific thought to some seriously silly questions because, as we know, science is fueled by curiosity.

SD: Of course. All right, so as our Muppet expert, I have to ask, if you had to put a label on Gonzo, what is he?

AC: Hmm. I think I would probably refer back to Muppet canon and say a whatever.

AC: Right. Well, in the 1981 film The Great Muppet Caper, a few of the Muppets get shipped to London in labeled crates. So Kermit’s says “frog,” Fozzie’s says “bear,” and Gonzo’s just says “whatever.”

AC: Very. But the Muppets haven’t always been super consistent with how they define what Gonzo is.

Three years earlier in the 1979 Muppet Movie, Kermit calls Gonzo sort of like a turkey. And then in 1999 in Muppets From Space, Gonzo was briefly labeled as an extraterrestrial.

AC: But for the most part, his species is left pretty ambiguous. It’s kind of become a running joke.

I may not have your Muppet know-how, but I can definitely ask experts some silly Muppet-related questions.

SD: So the first expert we consulted is Darren Naish, a paleontologist who studies extinct vertebrae anatomy, and Naish lines up a bit with Kermit’s turkey theory. He thinks Gonzo is a bird.

AC: A bird? So is he agreeing with Kermit’s turkey comment?

SD: Sort of. He looked at the evidence. Gonzo is fuzzy, so he’s likely warm-blooded. He’s got four limbs, a backbone, no teeth, and that curved beak-looking snout. And if you add all of those together, Naish says he can’t be anything other than a bird.

AC: Okay. I hear the logic, but I’m not fully abandoning my whatever theory just yet.

SD: Fair enough. Well, Naish actually got way more specific than a turkey. He looks at Gonzo’s slender, down-curving snout and sees an ibis, one of those long-billed wading birds.

AC: Okay, but ibises fly, and Gonzo only flies if he’s shot out of a cannon.

SD: Naish actually thought of that. It turns out birds lose flight all the time in evolutionary history. In fact, an extinct Jamaican ibis from about 10,000 years ago lost the ability to fly, and its wing bones actually evolved into heavy club-like weapons that it used to smack rivals in fights.

AC: Cool. They’re just swinging club hands in a brawl.

AC: I mean, honestly, that sounds extremely Gonzo. But not in a violent way. It’d be in a silly way. He’d be like-

SD: Of course, of course. So Naish’s theory is that Gonzo could be a highly derived flightless ibis.

AC: Okay. I kinda love that, but it still feels a little too normal for him.

SD: Well, hold onto your tuft of blue fuzz. Enter our second paleontologist, Thomas Holtz from the University of Maryland, who specializes in carnivorous dinosaurs. And Holtz looked at Gonzo and said, “You’re looking at the wrong geological era. Gonzo is actually way older, Jurassic kind of old.”

SD: A dinosaur. Holtz looked at Gonzo’s hands, and if you look at modern birds, their wing bones are fused together with drastically reduced digits. But Gonzo, Gonzo has three distinct, fully functioning, unfused fingers on each hand.

AC: True. I mean, he does have to hold his stunt props somehow.

SD: Exactly. And Holtz noted that Gonzo’s body is covered in simple down-like fuzz, with just a few complex feathers on his head. According to Holtz, you only see those two specific traits together, three free fingers and simple fuzzy coats, in early carnivorous dinosaurs from a group called Tetanurae.

AC: Tetanurae? What? Okay, who else is in that club?

SD: Oh, just the ancestors of raptors and early tyrannosaurs.

AC: No way. Tyrannosaurus rex? Is Gonzo related to a T-rex?

SD: Maybe. Holtz points out that other Muppets who are clearly birds, like Big Bird or Camilla and her chicken friends, have modern veined feathers and hard, shiny keratin beaks.

Gonzo has neither. So Holtz argues that if Gonzo is in the bird lineage, he split off tens of millions of years before modern feathers or fused wings ever evolved. He’s a living prehistoric relic.

SD: Yes. You got it. Your brain is doing fine.

SD: And to make matters even more confusing, though, Holtz points out the biggest scientific problem of all: Gonzo’s nose isn’t actually a beak at all.

SD: In birds and turtles, the beak is the mouth. It’s the actual jaw bone covered in hard keratin. But for Gonzo, that big purple nose thing is an extension sitting above and in front of his mouth. It doesn’t have the hard shine of keratin, and it doesn’t move like an elephant’s trunk. Holtz says it’s an anatomical structure that is basically unheard of in vertebrate biology.

AC: Leave it to Gonzo to have a face that literally defies anatomy. My whatever theory still holds water.

He pointed out that nobody asks what creature other Muppets like Animal or Elmo are because they don’t have distinct anatomical clues. But Gonzo has just enough real anatomy, feathers, a beak, three fingers, a chicken for a partner, to make our human brains desperate to categorize him. As Naish put it, “Specificity invites scrutiny.”

AC: And the more details you give us, the more obsessed we become with solving the puzzle.

SD: Exactly. So whether he’s an ibis, a dinosaur, or an evolutionary wild card, science still can’t give us a tidy one-word label.

AC: Which means, Sarah, there is only one logical thing left for us to do. We’ve heard what the paleontologists and the developmental biologists have to say, but what does the man behind the Muppet think?

AC: Truly a dream come true. That’s right after this quick break.

Welcome back. I am thrilled to welcome Muppet legend Dave Goelz. Dave has been the voice and spirit, I’d say, of Gonzo for 50 years. And then when we went on Sesame Street, this is before, before I was there, actually, they went on Sesame Street, they, it stayed with abstract characters, Ernie and Bert, Grover.

Grover is considered a monster. And they stayed with those abstract characters for quite a long time, and then when we did The Muppet Show, all of a sudden we were surprised to see pigs and chickens…

DG: I remember thinking, “This is weird, the Muppets are abstract. Why do we, why do we have a pig?” You know? “Why do, why do we have a chicken?” It was just an interesting transition ’cause that’s when we went more literal with, with species. Getting around to answering your question, I don’t know what Gonzo is. I have no idea. He was something that Jim built for a previous special, as you know, and when it came time to do The Muppet Show, Jim asked me to do this character who was kind of a loser outsider who does stupid acts and thinks they’re high art.

And then he asked for them to pull Gonzo out. Or that, that puppet that wasn’t Gonzo yet.

AC: What were your first impressions when you saw the puppet itself?

DG: Well, I had seen it before, so it wasn’t a surprise, but it was this pathetic-looking little guy, who had very downcast eyes. He was sort of limited, but I just started making a character out of him, and what my interest in him has always been is his character. And iin that one character, I found that it mirrored me. The reason that it did was because Jerry Juhl, who was our head writer and a very wise person and very funny and mischievous person, could see, I guess, that I was new.

I had no business in show business. I had no training. I had no acting training. We just started The Muppet Show, and Jim tossed me in, and I felt very out of place. I just go, “I don’t belong here. What am I doing in this room?” And so Jerry Juhl helped write Gonzo to be appropriate to where I was in life, and that was phase one. He was an outsider. He had a little bit of a baby talk accent…

DG: like a true newbie. And then as time went by, and I’m talking about years, I got more confident, and then one of our writers, Bill Prady, he started writing Gonzo as being very upbeat and enthusiastic. Like, “That is so cool,” you know, and, and just up for anything, and that became phase two of his character, which coincided with me being more comfortable in my new world And then phase three came when Jerry Juhl wanted to include Dickensian prose in the Muppet Christmas Carol film.

He needed that narrative prose in there, but didn’t want to have a narrator, and he had the idea, because we were very close friends, and he’d watched me go through therapy, and he’d watched me deepen and soften and evolve. He had the idea of letting Gonzo speak those lines.

AC: I feel like people have been asking this question since we all met Gonzo. Why do you think people care so much?

DG: Oh, I think I’ve learned a lot about that in the last, I don’t know, 10 years, let’s say. Whenever I appear at a museum or introduce a screening, people come up to me, and so many people come up and say, “Thank you. Gonzo gave me permission to be different.”

DG: He legitimized it. He made it cool. And a lot of these people are on the spectrum, and they are lovely people who have a hard time in life. And it was unintentional on my part. I didn’t know that they were, that Gonzo was having this effect on people, but he did.

And then about four months ago, I, I realized suddenly that, oh, wait a minute, no, no, this was unconscious on my part. I knew I was different. I didn’t belong in show business. I should be on my parents’ couch, you know, watching on the other end.

AC: Yeah, I feel like, I’m sure people have said this to you, you know, I think people think of Kermit as the heart of the Muppets, and they think of Gonzo as kind of the soul of the Muppets, and I think that nebulousness around what he is, of like not really knowing, I think it allows a lot of people, you know, myself included, that you can find a piece of yourself in him.

If you’ve ever felt excluded or weird, because he is not defined, there is lots of room to sort of hold a piece of him as a fan.

DG: Oh, Annie, that’s absolutely true. Absolutely true. He’s been that for people, and I have to say also that the Muppets as a whole are like that, too. They function the same way.

DG: Jim was a lover of characters. He hired characters. He hired all sorts of unusual people and found something for them to do and let them shine. It’s like I didn’t create Gonzo. It was me and the writers and Jim and the workshop. And these qualities exist in every single character, and there’s somebody out there who responds to every single one.

AC: You have a little bit of like an engineering and design background, right?

DG: I do, yeah. I was an industrial designer by training.

AC: Yeah, and I think especially lately there’s this sort of stark line between art and science, but you know, what we see, especially at Popular Science, is we see really amazing innovations can happen when art and science overlap.

So how do you bring a little bit of that engineering mind to playing a Muppet?

DG: A couple of things. First of all, when I first began, I already knew how to build puppets because I was trained as a designer at Art Center College of Design, and the design process was something that my dad inculcated into me, and then ArtCenter set in place.

And the design process that I use is about defining the problem, whether it’s a character, a performance, a glasses case, a typewriter. Whatever it is, it’s very important to know what the problem is, and it’s not always obvious. Listen, the reason I love that approach is that the more you hone in on the problem, the clearer the solution becomes.

AC: One final question. Because we’re Popular Science, I must ask about the Muppets’ preeminent scientist, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew-

AC: whom, of course, you also perform. If Bunsen, or Dr. Honeydew, he earned his degree, won a Nobel Prize, what do you think it would be for?

DG: Well, first of all, the idea is preposterous-

DG: On its face. That’s a great question. If he won a Noble Prize, what would it be for? A Nobel Peace Prize. All he’s done in life is make stupid inventions and hurt his assistant.

DG: So it really is a preposterous notion. I can’t even answer it.

I can’t. It’s just a mind-boggling question. I don’t have any idea how he could possibly be recognized for anything. I will tell you this, that Bunsen was, Bunsen was derived from a lot of scientists that I knew when I was in Silicon Valley. It wasn’t anybody directly, but it was this whole idea of being focused on electrons and being focused on tiny, tiny, very specific things, and losing the big picture.

DG: Yeah. ‘Cause it’s interesting you know, a scientist might be way deep into making a laser interferometer, and the science of it would be so riveting. And then my job was to come along and say, “Okay, what does it look like? How do you use it?” So I was, like, the user end of this whole deal. And, and so as a generalist, I could view the science world and the engineering world, and, uh, poke a little fun at it.

AC: Absolutely. Science is fun. We like to remind people.

AC: I will take off my journalist hat just for a second and say thank you so much for doing the podcast, but also just thank you so much for Gonzo. What you said about people who have maybe been called different or weird, it definitely resonates with me.

I’ve loved the Muppets my entire life, and being called weird my whole life is such a compliment because there’s so much joy and whimsy in the weirdos of Muppets, and Gonzo is such the epitome of that, that I thank you so much, Dave, for joining us today.

SD: Oh my gosh, was your inner Muppet heart exploding while talking to Dave? Yes. He seemed so wonderful.

AC: Yeah, he is just an absolute gem of a human. I did not even try to keep my fandom in check ’cause he’s a legend, and he’s genuinely meant so much to me as a Muppet fan.

SD: He’s the best. Oh my God. So after hearing from Dave and all of our biologists where do you, Muppet expert, officially land on the taxonomy of a Gonzo?

AC: Okay, I started the episode firmly on team whatever, but now I kinda love the idea that Camilla is casually dating a prehistoric dinosaur. But I also like the idea that Gonzo doesn’t have to be defined. He can be something different for everyone, like, whatever they need him to be.

SD: But the dinosaur theory does make his cannonball catching stunt seem a lot more on brand for a T-Rex relative.

And if you like our show, leave a rating and a review.

SD: Which Muppet do you want scientists to analyze next? Tell us in the comments. Please. Our producer is Alan Haburchak. This week’s episode was based on an article written for Popular Science by Niranjana Rajalakshmi, and a massive thank you to the legendary Dave Goelz for joining us.

AC: Thank you, team. Thank you, Dave, and thanks all you Muppets for listening.

SD: And one more time, if you want something you’ve always wondered about explained on a future episode, go to popsci.com/ask and click the Ask Us link. Until next time, stay weird wherever you are, and keep the questions coming.

#4501. 2028 Honda CR-V Will Go Hybrid-Only, Debut a New Platform

The new “Honda Hybrid” system is more efficient, increases power, and comes paired with an electric AWD setup.

We’re not done with 2026 quite yet, but the 2028 Honda CR-V is already coming in hot. On Thursday, the brand offered up its first official details about the next-gen version of the company’s highly important crossover—and big changes are in stow

First off, the 2028 model will be a complete redesign: underpinned by a new platform, boasting a fresh design inside and out, and powered by a new “Honda Hybrid” system. Not only is the hybrid new, but it will be the only powertrain choice available for the seventh-gen CR-V. This hybrid-only approach follows in the successful footsteps of the current Toyota RAV4, Honda’s biggest rival in the compact SUV segment.

When it comes to details, Honda is being purposely vague, but still giving us a few items to chew on. The new platform this CR-V will ride on increases body rigidity and reduces weight compared to the current car. It also has greater modularity built in, which Honda says will allow for greater parts commonality between models.

The Honda Hybrid powertrain itself will build on the two-motor hybrid system we’ve seen for years. Honda says it’s aiming for a 10-percent improvement to fuel efficiency gained by expanding the range where the engine operates most efficiently and an increase in the efficiency of the hybrid unit. More power is promised from the four-cylinder Atkinson cycle engine, and we’ll also see a new electric AWD system make its debut on this CR-V. Per usual, Honda is also claiming the CR-V will bring further enhancements to the “joy of driving,” which is always heartening to hear.

A single image of the new CR-V logo on a dark metallic blue paint was provided as a teaser. It’s rather edgy in appearance, far more so than the current logo’s font. We suspect this new sharper logo design will translate into the rest of the car, but Honda is holding back from showing us the SUV’s design for now.

This next-gen CR-V will continue to be built in North America with production spread out across three plants, two in the U.S. and one in Canada.

#4500. BYD and Geely approached FIA about a 12th F1 team, says Ben Sulayem

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio.

But there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.

“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem said of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.

He said he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a new one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the company to come back with a “serious proposal” that shows the project can work.

He also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.

Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

This isn’t new for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry, either by buying a team or building one from scratch.

In April, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”

Altavilla said BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.

Geely is the new name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.

The last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.

Here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.

The FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali says F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.

So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.

We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.

they look for visibility/recognition on the world stage, regardless EVs. And in some (primitive) markets they market themselves as hybrids automakers, not as EV automakers.

They will make a hybrid power unit (which they already make anyway) to comply with the backward F1 regulations.

But Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.

A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.

The bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.

If you’re following how fast EV tech is moving, from BYD’s batteries to F1’s hybrid power units, you can put some of that tech to work at home: pairing an EV with rooftop solar can cut your driving costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4499. 2026 kitchen gift guide: Essential cooking gear for chefs of every level

Updated Nov 13, 2026 10:58 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Someone doesn’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it. Having the right gear really helps, though, and that creates a wellspring of great gifting opportunities. The HORL3 Cruise holds a knife against a magnet at a fixed 15- or 20-degree angle while a diamond disc rolls along the edge. The ThermoWorks Thermapen Nano gets a reading in about 0.4 seconds, so anyone can stop guessing when a roast is done. The Challenger Bread Pan traps steam under a tall cast-iron lid, the same trick bakeries pull off with steam-injected ovens. Every pick below works on that principle, helping the home cook elevate their kitchen experience.

There are dozens and dozens of gifts here, grouped by category. Jump to: precision and measurement, knives and sharpening, pans and cookware, coffee, tea and drinks, baking and from scratch, countertop appliances, and cookbooks.

Seasoning a thick steak with a typical pepper grinder takes a lot of twisting. The MÄNNKITCHEN Pepper Cannon uses hardened high-carbon stainless steel burrs spinning on a drive shaft supported by two bearings inside a body milled from a solid block of anodized aluminum. MÄNNKITCHEN claims 10 times the output of top-rated mills, which it describes as seven cranks instead of 70. You set the grind from 8 to 60+ mesh with an adjuster on the base that clicks into spring-loaded detents. The hopper holds half a cup of peppercorns, and a removable cup underneath catches up to a third of a cup of ground pepper, which is handy when a rub calls for a measured amount.

A big mixing bowl tends to hide a kitchen scale’s display right when you need to read it. On the OXO Good Grips 11 lb Stainless Steel Food Scale with Pull-Out Display, the readout sits on a tray that slides out from the base, clear of whatever’s on the platform, then tucks back in for storage. It weighs up to 11 pounds (5 kilograms), and a meter on the display shows how much capacity you have left as you add ingredients. The display has an optional backlight, and the stainless steel platform lifts off so you can wash it by hand.

Sous vide cooking holds a water bath at the exact temperature you want your food to finish at, so a steak can sit in it and stay medium-rare instead of drifting toward well-done. The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 heats that bath with an 1,100-watt element and circulates 8 liters of water per minute, and Anova rates it to hold within 0.2°F anywhere from 32°F to 197°F. A two-line touchscreen on the cooker shows time and temperature, and dual-band Wi-Fi lets you start or check a cook from your phone. Anova gives it an IPX7 water-resistance rating, and the clamp adjusts and detaches to fit different pots.

ThermoWorks has closed out the Thermapen One, and the Thermapen Nano took its place this year. ThermoWorks rates the Nano’s fixed thermocouple probe for a full reading in 0.4 seconds and accuracy within 0.5°F between -4°F and 248°F, a window that covers everything from rare beef to pulled pork. Two magnets built into the body let it ride on the side of the fridge or range hood, and the display rotates a full 360 degrees, so the numbers read right-side up whichever hand you hold it in. It’s IP67 rated, runs roughly 1,000 hours on one AAA battery, and comes with a five-year warranty and a NIST-traceable calibration certificate.

A fast thermocouple thermometer doesn’t have to cost triple digits. TempPro, the brand formerly known as ThermoPro, builds a thermocouple sensor into the TempSwift Pro TP622 and rates it for a 0.1-second response time and accuracy within 0.5°F across -58°F to 572°F. That high end reaches past meat into frying oil and candy-making territory. The backlit display auto-rotates 180 degrees for left- or right-handed use, and the thermometer wakes up when you lift it and goes to sleep after 90 seconds of sitting still. It carries an IP65 water-resistance rating and runs on a single AAA battery.

The Combustion Predictive Thermometer (2nd Gen) is built around the question people actually ask during a roast: how much longer? Its probe carries eight sensors along its length, so the app can show the core, the surface and the air temperature around the food at the same time. Combustion’s prediction engine uses that heat-flow data to estimate the time remaining, and a feature it calls TrueCore reports the lowest internal reading even if you didn’t hit the center. Combustion rates the upper half of the probe to 900°F, so it can stay in a roast under the broiler or on the grill. Bluetooth reaches more than 330 feet in open air, and Wi-Fi requires a separate booster accessory.

Freehand sharpening is hard mostly because holding a steady angle is hard. The HORL3 Cruise takes that job off your hands: a magnetic block holds the knife at either 15 or 20 degrees, and you roll a wheel with a diamond disc back and forth along the edge. The other end of the roller carries a stainless steel honing disc to straighten and refine the edge you just ground. The Cruise’s body is made from ocean-bound recycled plastic, and HORL builds it in Germany. If the person you’re shopping for would rather have wood on the counter, the $179 HORL3 uses an oak or walnut body and swaps in an interchangeable ceramic disc.

STEELPORT forges its 8-inch Chef Knife from a single billet of American 52100 carbon steel in Portland, Oregon, then heat treats the edge and spine differently. The company says the edge ends up around 65 HRC, hard enough to take and hold a fine edge, while the spine stays below 30 HRC so the blade as a whole is less brittle. The handle is resin-stabilized Oregon bigleaf maple burl, and a magnetic walnut sheath comes in the box. Carbon steel picks up a patina and can rust, so wipe it dry after every wash. STEELPORT covers the knife with a lifetime warranty and sharpens it free for as long as you own it.

A knife that suddenly feels dull often has an edge that’s just rolled over, and a few passes on a honing rod push it back into line between real sharpenings. STEELPORT’s 12-Inch Oval Ceramic Honing Rod does that with a fine-grit ceramic surface over a steel core. The oval cross-section is there for contact, and STEELPORT says it puts more of the blade against the rod than a round one does. The rod measures 17 inches overall with a 5-inch contoured walnut handle and a finger guard, and it weighs 12 ounces. Ceramic can crack if it hits a tile floor, so give it a hook or its own drawer slot.

Shun builds the Classic 8-Inch Chef’s Knife around a VG-MAX steel core clad in 34 layers of stainless Damascus on each side, which is where the rippled pattern on the blade comes from. The core is hardened to 60-61 on the Rockwell scale and hand-sharpened to about 16 degrees per side, a fine edge that slices through onions and herbs cleanly. The full-tang blade sits in a D-shaped black PakkaWood handle, and the whole knife weighs 7.5 ounces. Shun makes it in Seki, Japan. A hard, thin edge like this one is happiest on a wood or plastic board, and it shouldn’t go anywhere near bones or frozen food.

Softer stainless steel is quicker to bring back to a sharp edge, and that’s part of the appeal of the Made In 8-Inch Chef Knife. It’s fully forged in Thiers, France, from nitrogen-treated X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58+ HRC, so a few passes on a whetstone or rolling sharpener refresh it. Made In grinds the edge asymmetrically, with a 14-degree primary bevel on one side and a 4-degree polishing bevel on the other, for 18 degrees total. The blade actually measures 8.5 inches and the knife weighs 7 ounces. If you order directly from Made In, the company will engrave it for $30 more, but engraved knives can’t be returned.

Someone outfitting a first real kitchen needs a handful of good knives more than a block with 15 slots. The Cangshan N1 Series 6-Piece Knife Block Set forges its blades from German X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58 HRC, a steel that’s easy to touch up at home. The N1’s signature is its patented all-metal hollow handle, which runs straight out of the blade, so there are no wood or plastic scales to crack or loosen. Cangshan sells the set under more than one model number, so check the knife list on the listing before you order.

Tojiro has renamed its long-running DP line to Classic, but the F-808 210mm gyuto itself didn’t change. It’s a san mai blade, with a VG10 stainless core hardened to about 60 HRC sandwiched between softer stainless outer layers that add toughness around the hard cutting steel. The 50/50 double-bevel edge suits right- and left-handed cooks equally, and the Western-style handle has a full tang, a stainless bolster and three rivets, so it’ll feel familiar to anyone coming from a German knife. Tojiro makes it in Tsubame-Sanjo, Japan. The edge measures 212 millimeters and the knife weighs 7.2 ounces.

Learning to sharpen on a stone starts with two grits, and the King KW-65 puts both on one block. The 1000-grit side does the sharpening and raises a fresh edge, then the 6000-grit side polishes it. It’s a soaking stone, so you submerge it for a couple of minutes before you start and keep it wet while you work. The muddy slurry that builds up on the surface helps it cut, so leave it there rather than rinsing it away mid-session. The stone measures about 7.3 by 2.5 by 1 inches, sits in an included plastic stand, and is made in Japan.

The deep, 6-quart sauté pan at the center of the All-Clad NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP comes with a steamer insert, a roasting rack and a tempered glass lid, so one piece of cookware can sear and steam on the stovetop or roast in the oven. The body is hard-anodized recycled aluminum, and a stainless steel base bonded underneath makes it work on induction burners. The ceramic nonstick interior is oven-safe to 450°F, though the lid tops out at 350°F and the pan can’t go under the broiler. Wash it by hand, and know that All-Clad’s warranty on this pan runs one year.

Carbon steel seasons and sears like cast iron, and it heats up and cools down faster when you adjust the burner. Made In’s Seasoned Carbon Steel Frying Pan arrives pre-seasoned with shea nut and coconut oils, so you can start cooking in it sooner than you could with a bare pan. The 12-inch size weighs 4.31 pounds, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2.25-inch sides. Made In builds it in Sweden, rates it for heat up to 1,200°F, and says it works on induction and over an open fire. The hollow stainless handle is designed to stay cool, and the pan should be washed by hand and dried right away.

Smithey is better known for cast iron, but its Deep Farmhouse Skillet is hand-forged carbon steel, made in Charleston, South Carolina. It’s about 12 inches across the top and 2 inches deep, which leaves room for a pan sauce or a shallow fry, and the cooking surface measures about 9.5 inches. Long handles on both sides stretch it to almost 21 inches end to end, so you can carry all 6 pounds of it to the table with two hands. Smithey lists it for use on gas, induction, electric and open fire.

Smithey’s 7.25 QT Dutch Oven skips enamel entirely. It’s bare cast iron with a fully polished interior, pre-seasoned with grapeseed oil, so it builds up seasoning the same way a skillet does and there’s no enamel coating to chip. The domed lid has drip channels on its underside that send condensation back down onto the food during a long braise. Expect some heft, since it weighs about 17.3 pounds with the lid. Smithey makes it in the US and backs it with a lifetime guarantee. Bare iron doesn’t love long simmers in tomato or wine, so save those braises for an enameled pot or keep them short.

Old cast iron is prized for its smooth, machined cooking surfaces, and Lancaster Cast Iron’s No. 8 Skillet brings that finish to a new pan. The cooking surface is polished smooth, then pre-seasoned with two layers of grapeseed oil at the company’s shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The No. 8 measures 10.5 inches across the top, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2-inch walls, and it weighs about 4 pounds. Polished iron starts out slick, and it gets slicker as layers of seasoning build up with every cook.

A saucier’s rounded bottom leaves no corners for a whisk or spatula to miss, which makes it the pan for custard and polenta and anything else that likes to scorch where the wall meets the floor. The Misen 3 QT Stainless Steel Saucier is 5-ply, with aluminum layers sandwiched inside stainless steel to spread heat across the base, and the walls are 3 millimeters thick. It measures about 9 inches across, comes with a lid, works on induction, and is oven-safe to 800°F. Misen backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects.

Kuhn Rikon’s 4th Burner Pot is tall and narrow, 5.5 inches across and holding 12 cups, so it fits on the small back burner while bigger pans take the front of the stove. That makes it handy for a couple of servings of pasta or a batch of blanched green beans. The glass lid has two built-in strainers and a pour spout, which lets you drain without hauling out a colander, and a removable basket inside handles steaming. Interior measurement marks save you a measuring cup, the silicone handles stay cool, and the stainless pot works on induction.

Microwave cooking goes better when steam is managed, and that’s the idea behind the Anyday 8-Piece Glass Round Dish Set. Each borosilicate glass dish gets a tempered glass lid with a silicone vent and gasket that let steam build and escape while the food cooks. Anyday says the stainless steel rim on each lid is microwave-safe as long as the dish sits at least an inch from the microwave’s walls. The set includes four dishes: two 4-cup sizes, one shallow and one deep, plus a 7-cup and an 8-cup. The bowls can go in the oven up to 500°F, so leftovers can get a crisp finish after they reheat.

Green tea scorches at a full boil, and pour-over coffee likes water a few degrees below it. The Fellow Corvo EKG Pro lets you dial in anywhere from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, then hold that temperature for 15 to 60 minutes so the second cup is as hot as the first. It also has an altitude setting, scheduling, and a pre-boil sanitize mode. The 0.9-liter body is 304 stainless steel. Fellow says the Wi-Fi only handles firmware updates, so you’ll still set the temperature on the kettle itself rather than from your phone.

Uneven grounds make uneven coffee, because the fine bits over-extract while the big chunks barely give up any flavor. The Fellow Ode Brew Grinder Gen 2 uses 64 mm stainless steel flat burrs, which cut a more uniform particle than the blade grinders most people start with. You get 11 settings split into 31 steps, a 100-gram capacity, and anti-static tech to keep grounds from clinging to the catch cup. Fellow built it for drip, pour-over, French press, and cold brew. It isn’t designed for espresso, so skip it for anyone pulling shots at home.

A coffee maker can only brew as well as its water temperature allows. The Moccamaster KBGV Select, handmade in the Netherlands, heats water quickly to brewing temperature with a copper boiling element, and the hot plate runs on its own separate element so it doesn’t cook the coffee sitting in the carafe. A switch on the brew basket adjusts the flow for a full 10-cup pot or a half batch, which keeps small batches from coming out thin. It carries the Specialty Coffee Association’s certification and a five-year warranty.

Most of the frustration of home espresso comes from dosing and grinding by feel. The Ninja Luxe Café Premier handles both: it has a conical burr grinder with 25 settings and a built-in scale that weighs the grounds for you, so each shot starts from a consistent dose. The Dual Froth System has four hands-free presets for steamed or frothed milk, and the machine also makes drip-style coffee and cold brew. It suits someone who wants café drinks without learning to tamp and time shots by eye.

So you know someone with a grinder, a pour-over cone, a French press, a cold brew pitcher, and a milk frother. But sometimes they need a coffee before they can face making coffee. And that’s where this indulgently overengineered Swiss superautomatic espresso maker comes in. The second-generation Z10 has a menu of 51 drinks you can choose and customize through the 4.3-inch touchscreen. Just pour beans in the hopper and fill the water tank. Drinks include classic hot options, as well as cold brew, which the first-gen could do by pulsing unheated water through a coarser grind. With milk or without. But now there are also light selections, plus caffeine regulation levels, as well as sweet foam picks (with a $35 chocolate attachment sold separately). And the upgraded P.R.G.2+ grinder resets itself for each offering, dialing in optimized granule consistency. Sure, it’s a splurge, but think of all the time and space someone will save replacing all those other coffee contraptions.

Most countertop carbonators tell you to fizz plain water and add flavor afterward, because carbonating juice or wine tends to foam over. The Drinkmate OmniFizz gets around that with what the company calls its Fizz Infuser cap, which releases pressure gradually so you can carbonate cold drinks other than water. It runs on standard 60-liter CO2 cylinders, and Drinkmate sells it alone or in bundles with extra cylinders. Check the bundles before buying, since the kits with more cylinders were sometimes cheaper than the smaller ones in early November.

Matcha powder starts losing its color and flavor once it’s ground, which is why the Cuzen Matcha Maker grinds whole tea leaves on demand. Its hopper holds up to 20 grams of leaf, and the machine mills it, then mixes it with water in the cup using a magnetic whisk. You can pick a 1-, 1.5-, or 2-gram shot depending on how strong you like it, and there’s a grind-only mode for baking or lattes. The Starter Kit comes with 4-gram samples of three Cuzen leaf blends and a brush for cleaning the mill.

Pod-based cocktail machines lock you into one company’s drinks. The Barsys 360 uses whatever you put in it: six 750-milliliter canisters hold your own spirits, juices, and syrups, and a Bluetooth app tells the machine how much of each to pour through the spouts over the glass. It doesn’t shake or stir, so plan on finishing drinks the old-fashioned way. It also runs on USB-C power and weighs about 10 pounds empty, which makes it easier than you’d expect to move from the counter to a party table.

Nugget ice, the soft, chewable kind, is made by compressing ice flakes rather than freezing cubes in a tray. The GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro does that on your counter, and Govee rates it for up to 60 pounds a day, with the first batch ready in about six minutes. A 4.9-liter side tank supplements the 2.2-liter main reservoir so you refill less often, and it has two self-cleaning cycles. You can also check on it or start it from the Govee app or by voice with Alexa or Google.

Centrifugal juicers spin produce against a fast blade, while slow juicers like the Hurom H310 Easy Clean press it with a turning screw at roughly 45 rotations per minute. Hurom’s version has a self-feeding hopper with a 50-millimeter chute that the company says fits whole apples, which cuts down on prep. Hurom backs the 150-watt motor with a 10-year warranty and covers the other parts for two years.

Boxed wine stays fresh longer than an open bottle, but the cardboard box is nobody’s idea of a centerpiece. The Boxxle Box Wine Dispenser is a stainless steel and ABS plastic housing for the bag inside a standard box. According to Boxxle, it lifts the bag so the spout sits above your glass and presses on the bag as it empties, so you can keep pouring until the last glass.

Fresh pasta dough needs to be rolled thin and evenly, and doing it with a rolling pin takes practice most people don’t have. The Marcato Atlas 150 is a hand-cranked roller with a 10-position thickness dial, so you can step the dough down a little at a time until it’s thin enough for lasagna sheets. The rollers are anodized aluminum, and the body is chrome-plated steel made in Italy. The version sold in the US includes fettuccine and spaghetti cutters, so you can go from sheet to noodles without buying attachments.

Most stand mixers drive a beater from above. The Ankarsrum Assistent Original flips that: its motor sits in the base and spins the 7-liter stainless steel bowl itself, while a dough hook or roller stays put. That design is why Ankarsrum says it can knead up to 5 kilograms of dough, a load that would stall a lot of tilt-head mixers. The Essential Package comes with a dough roller, dough knife, dough hook, spatula, and a proofing lid. Ankarsrum covers the base with a seven-year warranty, though accessories aren’t included.

Bread machines have a reputation for pale, unevenly baked tops. The Zojirushi Home Bakery Virtuoso Plus adds a heater in the lid to go with the usual one underneath, so the top of the loaf browns along with the sides. It bakes a 2-pound loaf and uses two kneading blades, which helps it work a full 2-pound batch of dough evenly.

Sourdough gets its crackly crust from steam trapped around the loaf early in the bake, which is why so many bakers use a Dutch oven. The Challenger Bread Pan rearranges that idea: you set the dough on a shallow cast-iron base and lower a tall domed lid over it, so you’re not dropping a floppy loaf into a deep, 500-degree pot. It weighs 20 pounds, is made in the USA, and is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. Its 15.5-by-10.5-inch footprint fits oblong batards as well as round boules.

HexClad’s hybrid surface finally made the jump from frying pans to the oven. The HexClad Hybrid Baking Sheets use the same pattern of raised stainless steel hexagons with nonstick valleys in between, built over 2.5-millimeter tri-ply with an aluminum core. HexClad says the ceramic coating is free of PFAS and rates the sheets for oven temperatures up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re sold in two-packs in small and medium sizes, and the medium sheet measures 10 by 15 inches. HexClad says they’re dishwasher-safe but recommends washing them by hand.

Detroit-style pizza owes its crunchy, cheese-crisped edges to a deep rectangular pan that conducts heat fast. The LloydPans 10×14 Detroit-Style Pizza Pan is 2.5 inches deep and made from 14-gauge anodized aluminum in Spokane Valley, Washington. Its Pre-Seasoned Tuff-Kote finish means you can skip seasoning and use metal utensils on it, according to LloydPans. Spread the cheese all the way to the edges so it melts down the sides and fries against the metal.

Stretching pizza dough on a countertop usually ends with flour everywhere. The Gozney Pizza Prep Board has raised edges that keep the flour on the board and a catch tray at the back where you can sweep extra flour and reuse it. Its textured surface holds a thin, even coating of flour, which Gozney says works better than wood, steel, or marble at keeping dough from sticking and tearing on its way to the peel. A bench hook keeps it from sliding, and size markings go up to 16 inches. It’s 22 by 21.5 inches, so check counter space first.

Neapolitan pizza wants a stone near 850 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature home ovens don’t reach. The Ooni Volt 2, successor to the Volt 12, gets there on a standard 120-volt outlet in about 20 minutes, according to Ooni. Inside is a 10-millimeter cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pizzas, and Ooni’s Pizza Intelligence system shifts power between the heating elements as you cook. Presets cover Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan pizza. At about 39 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you’ll want to give it a permanent spot.

Chef Nancy Silverton started with a quarter sheet pan when she helped Made In design this dish, then stretched it longer and wider. The Made In Porcelain Baking Slab is a 9-by-13-inch French porcelain dish fired three times in the Loire Valley, with a lower profile than a typical casserole so roasted vegetables and gratins get more browning. It’s oven-safe to 650 degrees Fahrenheit and microwave-safe, and it weighs 3.8 pounds. Made In’s care guide says it can go in the dishwasher, though the company’s FAQ recommends hand washing.

Most microwaves cook by guesswork, and the most interaction you have is five beeps and the sighs/screams when things are too cold in the middle and hot at the edges. This sleek Japanese Microwave from Panasonic, however, uses its new Genius Sensor 2.0 to constantly measure 64 points on your food’s surface every 0.1 seconds, so one button push can achieve even temperature throughout a plate of mixed leftovers. And steady inverter power ensures the center heats, too. The drop-down door, like a wall oven, suits even a narrow galley kitchen (aka many Asian apartments), while the flat, turntable-free interior can fit up to a 9-by-13 dish. This recent import is a 2026 Red Dot Design winner for a reason: it’s got a look as tasty as your bowl of steamy soup.

Want that perfectly fluffy restaurant rice at home, but without under- or over-cooking anxiety and hot-spot drama? Get a Zojirushi rice cooker. I’ve given the NS-ZCC10 Neuro Fuzzy Logic model as a graduation/housewarming gift multiple times because I knew from personal experience it delivers year after year. Then I got this pressure + induction cooker in 2025 and daaaaaaamn … somehow the best got better. Sticky-plump sushi or stir-fry grains, pleasingly textured oatmeal, brown rice that doesn’t take all of eternity. No sad, beige cement. This tiny, calm chef quietly adjusts the heat to deliver evenly cooked everything. It’s not as fast as some cookers, but it beats them in consistency. Fill to the line, press a button, go live life, come back to perfection. This is an upgrade that quietly, magically improves your entire kitchen rhythm.

Coffee nerds have so much in common with audiophiles. Both are obsessed with micro-calibrated gear and swapping components in and out in the pursuit of clarity. So if you know someone as obsessed with puck preparation as they are running a carbon-fiber anti-static brush over every album, you know someone who needs the Mazzer Philos premium light commercial single-dose grinder. Like a summit-fi digital audio converter, this $1,495 hand-assembled, heirloom-quality Italian appliance (available in black and silver) takes whatever beans it’s fed and extracts previously masked tasting notes with minimal morning commotion. A wide dial covers espresso to pour-over to batch brew coarseness, and the near-zero-retention vertical burr + chute knocker + Dose Finisher system lets you move between origins and brewing methods without yesterday’s beans staging a comeback. Swappable 64mm flat burrs give someone a chance to tune for vibrant light and full-bodied dark roasts, and the option to switch from stepped to stepless mode gives grind settings the same obsessive precision as establishing the perfect listening position.

Nik Sharma’s newest book builds its 100 recipes around the science of flavor, explaining why each technique works. Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking came out from Chronicle Books in September 2026. It’s a good fit for the cook who keeps asking why a recipe calls for a specific step, and wants the answer along with dinner.

#4498. Every EV from Every Brand in America

We've created this handy guide to let you know all the brands that sell electric vehicles in the United States.

While gas-powered vehicles still make up an overwhelming majority of cars sold in the United States, their market share is slowly getting chipped away at by battery-electric ones. Since the Nissan Leaf and Tesla Roadster brought electric vehicles back to the national stage in the late 2000s, automakers have worked overtime to noticeably improve the charging speeds and driving ranges of their battery-powered products. No longer limited to small cars, EVs now take up space in just about every automotive segment.

We've compiled an exhaustive list of today's options to make it easy to determine what electric vehicles are available from which automotive brands in the United States. Don't go looking for hydrogen-powered electric vehicles here, though, as we've excluded those from this list.

Audi sells an array of electric SUVs and cars, from the compact Q4 e-tron to the range-topping 912-hp RS e-tron GT. Both of Audi's electric SUVs are available in either wagon or fastback body styles.

BMW's EV sedans look similar to their gas-powered cars, but the iX3 and incoming i3 promise next-generation looks and technology.

Cadillac's lineup of electric vehicles consists of an SUV in nearly every size, including the Escalade IQ, which looks just as ostentatious as the gas-powered Escalade despite its silent powertrain.

Chevrolet's electric vehicle arsenal is centered around SUVs, but the American automaker also caters to business owners with the WT version of the Silverado EV pickup truck.

Dodge currently sells just one EV, the Charger Daytona, which is available as either a coupe or sedan. It assumes the muscle car role vacated by the previous Scat Pack and Hellcat versions of the Charger and Challenger.

The only Fiat sold in the United States right now is an electric version of the company's iconic 500 city car. Fiat also offers the Topolino, which is technically classified as a "Low Speed Vehicle" and is limited to 25 mph.

Ford sells two electric models, the Mustang Mach-E SUV and the E-Transit commercial van.

The Genesis Electrified GV70 is based on the Korean automaker's popular compact SUV, while the GV60 utilizes the same platform found under the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6.

GMC's lineup of electric vehicles is just as big and brash as its gas-powered offerings. Two pickups and an SUV are available.

Hyundai has won Car and Driver's EV of the Year award three times in a row, first with the Ioniq 5 SUV in 2022 and then with the Ioniq 6 sedan in 2023. The high-powered Ioniq 5 N, which entertains with faux gearshifts and engine noises, won the award in 2024.

Jeep currently sells two EVs in the U.S. Although the Wagoneer S shares the first part of its name with the gas-powered Wagoneer, the EV is completely unrelated to that behemoth. The Recon is an electric alternative to the off-road-ready Wrangler.

Kia's lineup of EVs currently consists of a trio of SUVs.

Lexus currently sells two EVs in the United States: the RZ SUV, which is related to the Toyota bZ, and an electric version of the ES sedan.

California-based startup Lucid Motors exclusively builds EVs and recently launched its second model, the Gravity SUV.

The Italian luxury brand currently offers three EVs in the U.S., all of which are related to the brand's gas-powered models and carry the Folgore suffix to distinguish them as battery-powered.

Mercedes offers a vast range of EVs, from sedans to SUVs and even vans. The automaker has begun shifting away from its "EQ" naming structure for EVs, starting with the electric G-class, which dons the name G580 with EQ Technology. It's a wordy solution that'll also appear on the upcoming battery-electric 2026 CLA-class.

While Mini previously sold an electric variation of its iconic Cooper hatchback, the latest version has been delayed indefinitely, meaning Mini currently offers just one EV in the U.S., a battery-powered variant of its Countryman SUV

Nissan sells one EV in the United States, the Leaf, which has transformed from a hatchback to an SUV for its third generation.

There are currently three Porsche EVs on sale in the U.S., with an electric successor to its 718 sports car on the way.

Ram, the truck division spun off from Dodge in 2009, currently sells one EV. Ram had originally aimed to start building the 1500 REV in late 2024 for deliveries in early 2025, but the electric pickup truck is now delayed to late 2026.

Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan.

#4497. Watch BYD’s robotic charging arm plug itself in and charge EVs in 5 minutes [Video]

BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.

After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its new ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.

The Chinese automaker launched a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.

In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.

The new charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

The new robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.

By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD said the new tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.

Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.

A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez)

Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the new charging tech in action.

The integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.

If they could tie this into a smart summon type of capability, where the vehicle communicates with the charger and moves the vehicle into the proper location for charging and then moves to a parking spot once charging is complete. Rental car fleets would benefit and so would those in shopping centers. There are so many possibilities and this looks far more mature that the old snake charging Tesla demoed.

BYD has over 16 years of experience in the solar industry with a portfolio that includes solar cells, modules, and systems.

Its solar division, BYD Solar, does business in over 100 countries and regions. By using solar power, BYD said, the SCC system can operate independently off-the-grid.

The new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.
