#4424. Peek Inside the Ford Vault, a New Museum Housing the Best From Ford and Lincoln

The Vault will eventually open to public eyes, and it’ll be worth a visit once it does.

For decades, Ford’s internal policy was to not keep examples of cars it’s made. Once their useful lifespan was up, they were to be sold, donated, or trashed. That being the case, there’s never been an official museum of cars past and present operated by the Blue Oval here in the U.S. Until now, that is. Say hi to the Ford Vault.

In the same sense that Porsche has the Porsche Museum and Mercedes-Benz has the Mercedes-Benz Museum, the Ford Vault is a place to admire the long history of Ford and Lincoln. It’s not open to the general public yet – Ford intends to ultimately open its doors to anyone – but we got a sneak preview of what to expect when Ford’s finished with this large hall of vehicles.

As of now, there are 125 cars and trucks inside this warehouse-like building in Romulus, Michigan. Situated about 20 or so miles from Ford World Headquarters in Dearborn, this only exists because of Jim Farley’s blessing. Thanks to orders from the top to change Ford’s vehicle retention policy, a collection of historical vehicles finally became possible. It’s taken about three years of buying special vehicles and unearthing some that were squirreled away, but Ford finally has an array of cars worth showing off. A small fraction of them (about 15 at this stage) are on loan from folks happy to show their cars off in Ford’s space. It’s a practice that Ford says it intends to continue, giving new visitors something fresh to see each time they return.

We got a chance to walk through the Vault this week. Read on for some highlights of what you can expect should you find yourself in the Ford Vault one day.

This Mustang doesn’t look like much from the outside, but it houses one of the most ambitious skunkworks engine projects from Ford that never made it past the prototype phase. Back when Ford was developing the 2005 Ford GT, it was searching for the right powertrain for the job. Engineers thought a V-10 could fit the bill, so it combined two modular 4.6-liter V-8 engine blocks to create a short deck V-10 measuring 351 cubic inches. Hilariously, it fit in the engine bay of the Mustang. This prototype in particular has been kept off the books for decades since to ensure it lived on, and now it’s proudly displayed in the Vault.

Speaking of Ford GTs, the Vault is home to a huge number of them. One of the particularly special ones is this concept that debuted at the 2002 Detroit Auto Show. Nicknamed “Petunia,” it’s an example of a concept that was truly representative of the production car to follow. That said, look close, and you’ll spot the differences. The headlight and fog light designs, for instance, are different on the final car. Same goes for various vents and openings throughout the body. It’s close, but not identical to the 2005 GT that came out a few years later.

The Ka being present here in the Vault foreshadows that it won’t just be American-sold Fords and Lincolns that will make their way into the collection. This particular Ka is the last first-gen example to roll off the line, and it has less than 10 miles on the odometer. It’s also a charming aside from the barrage of Ford Mustangs and GTs on display here.

These three are on loan to Ford for the time being to coincide with the launch of the brand’s new Le Mans Hypercar. As you likely already know, they’re the three GT40s that swept the podium at the 1966 Le Mans. Ford rightly has them lined up in the feature spot inside the Vault. There’s no guarantee these pieces of history will be there when Ford decides to open up to the public, but it sure is a great way to kick this collection off with a bang.

Ford has about 30 different concept cars from across the years on display right now, and one of the funkiest is the Ute Concept. Ford’s EVB Metal Shop crafted this creation using a Ranger bed and the original Mustang decklid as the tailgate. Obviously, it was only ever made as a one-off.

Again, it’s not all Mustangs and GTs, and thankfully, Ford found some space for its affordable, entry-level enthusiast cars. Not pictured here, but across the hall, Ford has both a Fiesta ST and Focus ST on display, too. It’s not often you see perfectly kept Focus and Contour SVTs, so it’s great to see Ford found some to preserve.

It’s not just on-road race cars that made the cut for the Vault, and Ford found a special one with this Baja 1000 Bronco. Prepared by Bill Stroppe for the 1967 Mexican 1000, it’s the first of four Broncos that Stroppe built to compete in off-road rallies and competitions. You might recall its color scheme from today’s Bronco Stroppe Edition made as a tribute to the original truck.

Leno has an absurd number of cars, but did you ever wonder which was his first? That would be a 1934 Ford Pickup, and while the one seen here isn’t the car, it’s an example he bought about 10 years ago to mimic his original. Ford is keeping it safe and dry for Leno for the time being, but it will eventually be shipped back out to California for a future episode of Jay Leno’s Garage.

Ford is seemingly bringing back the Cobra name in a big way soon, and it’s highlighting the trim’s history with a collection of three Cobra Rs here at the Vault. Each one of these Cobra Rs (1993, 1995, and 2000) are the first production examples off the line for each generation. The 2000 Cobra R with its big wing and independent rear suspension is the most well-known of the bunch, and we have high expectations for the continuation of the Cobra line.

#4423. The $700,000 Audi Nuvolari Will Be Extremely Rare in the U.S.

Audi has announced the official price for its brutalist supercar in the U.S. and confirmed that owners will have to wait until 2028 to receive their Nuvolari.

Three years after the death of the R8, Audi revealed a new supercar. First shown in June, the Nuvolari wears a brutalist design and borrows the Lamborghini Temerario’s 789-hp twin-turbo V-8, mating it with a trio of electric motors for a total of 987 horsepower. Unlike the R8, though, the Nuvolari will be a limited-production affair, and now we know just how many will make it to the United States, and what they’ll cost when they get here.

The R8, which lasted from 2007 to 2023, was a true series production car, but Audi only plans on building 499 units of the Nuvolari. Of that total, just 182 will reach the United States. Once they do, each of their new owners will have to pony up at least $700,000. That figure doesn’t include the designation fee, which Audi has yet to disclose.

The lucky few who get to park a Nuvolari in their garage (or more likely a supercar-filled warehouse) will have to be patient. Deliveries won’t start until the first half of 2028, but once owners get their hands on the Nuvolari, we imagine they will be quite happy. That 987-hp powertrain propels the distinctively designed supercar to 60 mph in a claimed 2.5 seconds and to a top speed of 217 mph, making it both the most powerful and fastest production Audi ever.

#4422. BYD’s new 5-seat luxury SUV brings big screens, big range, and starts at about $40,000

BYD launched the Denza N8 EV in China, a five-seat luxury SUV that promises more than 1,000 km (621 miles) of CLTC range, a tech-filled cabin, and plenty of premium extras.

Another day, another new BYD vehicle is now on sale in China. After opening preorders for the Denza N8 EV a few weeks ago, BYD held the grand launch event on Thursday.

The new N8 EV, or “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza called it, is available in six variants, including four battery-electric (EV) and two plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain options.

The all-electric Denza N8 starts at 269,900 yuan, or about $40,500, with prices ranging up to 329,900 yuan ($49,500) for the Flagship model. The PHEV models start at 300,900 yuan and 32,900 yuan, respectively.

Measuring 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, the Denza N8 EV is slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

Inside, the interior is pretty over the top with a huge 30″ panoramic infotainment screen that stretches nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard. There’s also a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

BYD added a few premium extras like front and rear zero-gravity seats, a drop-down ceiling entertainment screen, ambient lighting, and wireless phone chargers.

The Denza N8 is offered with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD variant uses a single motor that delivers either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp), depending on the configuration.

The tri-motor Denza N8 debuts BYD’s e3 Evo technology. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

BYD’s Denza said the N8 EV boasts an all-electric CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles), “making it the world’s longest-range mass-produced all-electric SUV.”

To put it in perspective, that’s as much as the outgoing N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

It’s available with two second-gen BYD Blade battery packs: 105.792 kWh and 130.15 kWh, delivering CLTC ranges of up to 885 km (549 miles) and 1,003 km (623 miles).

With BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, the Denza N8 EV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. Charging from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Like many of its new luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is equipped with BYD’s premium tech and features, such as its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system and God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system.

BYD also sells the extended Denza N8L in China, which went on sale earlier this year, starting at 299,800 yuan ($45,000).

#4421. BYD's Futuristic EV Charger Can Run On Sunshine And Batteries

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BYD has already shown that charging an EV doesn’t have to take much longer than filling a gas tank. Now it’s tackling another problem: getting enough electricity to a fast charger in the first place.

Its new site in the Abu Dhabi desert combines solar panels, battery storage, Flash Charging, and a robotic arm that plugs in the car. BYD says the system can work independently of the electricity grid, potentially bringing fast charging to places where a power connection may not be feasible. The proposition is pretty simple: Solar panels generate electricity, batteries store it, and the charger sends it to an EV.

Battery-backed charging is becoming more common because it lets stations deliver more power than their grid connection alone can supply, while also reducing demand on the grid during busy periods. Tesla’s biggest Supercharger site, which it opened earlier this year, also uses solar panels and Tesla's Megapack batteries. Companies like Electric Era and Beam Global specialize in battery-backed charging. Even BYD Flash chargers not located in the middle of the desert and not supplied by solar panels use on-site energy storage to boost power delivery.

Each of BYD's T-shaped Flash chargers is hooked up to two 185-kilowatt-hour storage batteries, for 370 kWh total. These draw power from the grid at around 100 to 560 kilowatts, then supply the car at a much higher rate. The chargers can send up to 1,500 kW through one cable, or up to 1,000 kW when both are in use at the same time.

Adding solar panels into the equation means some or even all of that electricity can be generated on-site. However, BYD hasn’t disclosed the battery capacity or solar output of this new desert installation. So it's not clear how many cars the station can charge—or how quickly—on solar power alone.

The charging hardware is impressively quick. With BYD’s latest 1,500-kW Flash chargers, compatible cars running its second-generation Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or hit 97% in nine minutes.

Now that infrastructure is going global. The company says it plans to establish 6,000 Flash Charging stations worldwide by the end of 2027, but it hasn’t specified how many will offer solar power, off-grid operation, or that robotic arm.

Europe is getting a taste of BYD’s Flash charging with sites up and running in Italy, Germany, France, and the United Kingdom. Canada is coming soon too. The only vehicle it currently sells in Europe that can fully utilize its power is the Denza Z9 GT. During a demonstration, the electric wagon charged from 10% to 80% in six minutes and 32 seconds, reaching 97% in nine minutes and 22 seconds.

#4418. Scout's New Factory Is Already Making Trucks. But You Won't Be Able To Buy One For A While

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Scout's new South Carolina factory has started producing vehicles, the company announced Thursday. They're not production cars, and they're not for sale, but it's a big step on the company's path to market.

The factory is now building validation vehicles that will be used for further development. That means they'll be undergoing real-world testing and refinement, and be used to iterate the production process and final vehicle design.

The company has about a year to learn those lessons before it is supposed to start producing final, sellable models. It has said that production of sellable vehicles will begin next year, with first deliveries set for 2028. In a world where so many EVs have been delayed or canceled, too, the company is publicly signaling its intent to deliver.

That doesn't mean it's been an easy road. The company's "Harvester" extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) have proven far more popular among pre-orderers than the company expected, with the vast majority of reservation holders skipping the purely electric option. That's why the range-extended Traveler SUV will launch first, followed by the Terra pickup and pure-electric models. Like most automakers, the company seems to have overestimated demand for the pure electric models when it was initially announced.

The entire segment has largely been creamed. The two most popular all-electric truck models—the Ford F-150 Lightning and Tesla Cybertruck—have both been canceled as of last week. Buyers have proven unwilling to pay a large premium for purely electric trucks. That's why Ram killed its all-electric truck program in favor of an upcoming EREV truck, why the next Lightning will get a range extender, and why Scout is focusing on the Harvester models.

But that market is also unproven. Ram's EREV has been delayed a number of times, and the Scout and Ford remain a ways off. The question is whether EREVs can overcome the pricing challenges that electric trucks have faced without compromising on utility or range. Given that all of these brands are planning to over over 500 miles of range on a full battery and a full tank, I don't expect usability issues. Until we see detailed pricing, though, it's hard to know how big of a market this will be.

Regardless, Scout has a lot of advantages. It has the backing of Volkswagen, an automotive giant. It will benefit from that company's tie-up with Rivian, which should lead to excellent software and lower production costs. And it's using a great name in a real niche: proper off-road, solid-axle trucks and SUVs. Add in a bench seat and a great design and you certainly have my interest.

But as we've seen time and time again, actually launching a new brand is tough. The company has to navigate a flurry of dealer lawsuits and a challenging automotive environment, all while sustaining our interest for another year. It's far from a guaranteed success. But today, Scout got a bit closer to the finish line.

#4415. Laid-Off Id Software Employees Form their Own Studio, Hidden Horses

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

2026 has been home to a swath of large-scale layoffs throughout the gaming industry, mostly in the western sector. A statistically-significant portion of these layoffs have come from Microsoft, which has been systematically pruning many of its subsidiaries, including some of its highest-profile studios like id Software and Bethesda. Obviously, this is terrible for the many, many developers who worked for those studios, but some of those same developers have decided to turn this pinch into a chance.

Xbox cut 3,200 jobs. The developers who lost theirs explain what that actually means for the games that were supposed to come next.

Today, a coalition of developers who were specifically laid off from id Software following their work on Doom: The Dark Ages announced the formation of their new independent studio: Hidden Horses. If that name is a reference to something, I don’t know what it is, but what this studio may lack in readily-apparent branding, it more than makes up for in the crew of talented, highly-experienced developers it consists of.

According to Hidden Horses’s newly-created website, this independent studio wants to make games “like it was done in the 90’s,” with an emphasis on carefully hand-crafted gaming experiences tailored by longtime industry veterans. The studio’s first project is already in progress, with plans to bring it to life via crowdfunding in the near future.

While these industry vets have lost the ample funding that comes with a major backer like Microsoft, they have, in turn, gained substantial freedom in how they pursue their projects. This is one of the stated benefits of the studio’s formation, as outlined on the “How We Work” section of the Hidden Horses website.

“The company was created as a developer run and owned studio,” the page reads. “This allows us to pursue fun and creativity in our games, unencumbered by short-term thinking or chasing market trends.”

They have gained substantial freedom in how they pursue their projects.

The team considers this structure optimal because helps them make games right, rather than make them quickly, creating new and interesting gameplay concepts rather than trying to flip half-baked products for a quick buck. The team is firmly of the belief that, despite changes in the industry and players, there is still very much a demand for the kinds of carefully-designed games that they’re accustomed to creating.

After being cut off by its previous publisher, Romero Games has secured a fresh bout of funding and refocused with a smaller dev team.

The page also notes that the studio will be run democratically, with input from every member of the team on all important business decisions, all to ensure nobody gets left out in the cold. “We do this not only because we think it is fair, but because we think it is a better way to run a business.”

Despite having just formed, Hidden Horses already has irons in the fire. On the “Our First Project” page of the website, the studio outlines its plans for its very first game development project. This game, titled Danger Pay, will be a “high-octane single-player FPS” set in a malevolent, futuristic game show in a manner reminiscent of Smash TV and The Running Man.

“Our game will focus on classic FPS gameplay, awesome weapons, crazy enemies, and will be highly optimized.”

Of course, financial backing for an entirely new game project doesn’t come out of nowhere, which is why the plan for this first project is to fund it via Kickstarter. A page for Danger Pay has already been created, though there’s no word yet on when the campaign will actually begin.

“We believe that the community around the type of games we have helped develop is robust, and we invite all supporters to join us in trying to create something special,” the Kickstarter description reads. “This will include the typical things needed to start a business and finance a game's development - licenses, hardware, healthcare, etc. Our goal will be based around the timeline of our first project and associated costs.”

You can now experience Wyldheart, the upcoming co-op RPG from former AAA developers, for yourself.

#4414. America's Top 3 SUVs Are About To Be Hybrid Or Electric

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Recent moves from Toyota and Honda prove it once and for all: Pure gasoline options just can't hang with electrified power anymore. On Thursday, Honda announced that its best-selling CR-V crossover will be available exclusively as a hybrid starting with a redesigned 2028 model.

"With a 100% hybrid powertrain, the next-generation Honda CR-V will further expand the appeal of America's most popular SUV as demand for hybrid-electric vehicles reaches record levels," said Luis Guerra, assistant vice president of Honda National Auto Sales.

Arriving next year, the 2028 CR-V will kick off a seventh generation for the SUV and be powered exclusively by a new two-motor hybrid system. Honda says the tech will boost driving efficiency and expand the range where the engine operates most efficiently, as compared with its current hybrid system. Today, the CR-V is available with both hybrid and pure-combustion powertrains.

Toyota made the RAV4 exclusively a hybrid starting with the 2026 model. Now Honda is following suit.

The Honda news follows similar decisions by Toyota, which made the RAV4 SUV hybrid-only starting with the 2026 model. (The Camry, too, is now only a hybrid.)

Taken together, it means that soon the top three models in the heart of the U.S. car market will come with some form of electrification. That alone will do a lot for getting people into more efficient cars—even if they aren't ready for an EV yet. In 2025, the RAV4, CR-V, and Tesla Model Y were America's best-selling SUVs, responsible for some 1.2 million sales combined.

The move should give a further boost to hybrid sales in America, which have already been on a tear. In the third quarter, hybrids reached 16% of the U.S. light-duty vehicle market. Chalk it up to growing awareness, higher gas prices, and more options in the marketplace.

Those options are poised to grow even further as more automakers capitalize on growing interest in hybrids—particularly in the SUV segment. Nissan is readying a Rogue Hybrid with a unique hybrid system that makes it drive a lot like an EV. GM is reportedly bringing hybrid powertrains to its three-row SUVs, like the Chevy Traverse and GMC Acadia.

In a sense, it's a wonder the hybrid boom didn't happen sooner. Getting a hybrid instead of a gas vehicle is essentially a no-brainer. You may pay a little more up front, but research shows that the fuel savings over time pay off the difference fairly quickly. According to Consumer Reports, the average hybrid commands a $1,700 premium, but most models pay for themselves within four years.

Just remember: Full EVs are still the cheapest vehicles to run per mile, if you have home charging. They'll always be better for the environment than hybrids too. And the smooth, quiet driving experience is tough to beat. More hybrid Hondas are a step in the right direction, but with the automaker bowing out of the EV game for now, buyers looking to ditch gas entirely will have to look elsewhere.

#4413. SpaceX could announce $1.5 trillion Tesla merger in December: report

Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination. A deal could be announced as soon as December, which would make it the largest merger ever, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.

According to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved. December is the target, but early 2027 is also on the table.

One of the variables on the table is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive. So, as expected, this is shaping up as SpaceX absorbing Tesla, not the other way around.

That fits the valuations. SpaceX is worth over $1.9 trillion after its June IPO, while Tesla sits around $1.5 trillion. For scale, the record for a single deal has long been Vodafone’s $183 billion takeover of Mannesmann in 2000, and even SpaceX’s roughly $250 billion purchase of xAI (a private company at the time) earlier this year would be dwarfed.

Neither company commented. Tesla stock rose as much as 1.9% on the report.

We’ve been tracking this since May, when Musk first floated merging the two companies weeks before the SpaceX IPO. At the time, we called it the fourth time Musk would make a more than $1 billion self-dealing transaction, after SolarCity, Twitter/X, and Tesla’s $2 billion xAI investment that turned into SpaceX stock.

Then, in October, Tesla’s proxy filing read like a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees, has sat on SpaceX’s board since February. The ballot for the December 3 meeting is limited to re-electing Musk, chair Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to terms through 2029, plus a say-on-pay vote and the auditor.

A day later, Musk confirmed that both boards had formed special committees to explore a merger.

The governance piece is where Tesla shareholders should pay the most attention.

Musk owns about 20% of Tesla but controlled roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares, according to its S-1. Swapping Tesla shares for SpaceX shares means trading one-share-one-vote for a company where Musk’s control is effectively locked in.

And the deal itself pays Musk. Under the change-in-control terms in his 2025 CEO award, the operational milestones drop out and the market cap test runs at the deal price, with earned shares vesting immediately. Based on the share count in the proxy, a deal valuing Tesla at $2 trillion (about a 33% premium to where it trades now) would clear the first market cap tranche on the spot. His 286 million restricted shares from the 2018 package also accelerate on a change in control.

Bloomberg reports that one of the main obstacles is how to ring-fence Tesla’s China business. A JPMorgan analyst described SpaceX’s defense and government work and Tesla’s China footprint as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulators and shareholders.

That’s the same issue behind the Wall Street Journal’s July report that Tesla was weighing a sale or spinoff of its China operations, which Musk denied. Giga Shanghai is Tesla’s most productive factory and builds more than half of its cars. It shipped 67,829 vehicles in October alone.

Politics is the other wild card. Congress flipped to Democrats in the midterms, and they’ve said Musk’s companies and his political ties will get a hard look. Bloomberg previously reported the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

I suspected that the midterms might accelerate the timeline. The Dems don’t take office until January, and Musk likely wants to move this as far along as possible before then.

No rational independent board would offer $1.5 trillion (much less $2 trillion) for Tesla. It is a shrinking EV company with a few fantasy projects that are not delivering. But endlessly diluting other stockholders is his thing.

As for the “independent committees”, those are obviously a joke. No one believes that, but it’s not like Tesla’s shareholders would care at this point. Tesla’s stock has been a dud for 4 years, and shareholders’ best chance to see a return is another self-deal with Musk.

Tesla is a car and energy company with falling car sales, and it would get folded into a rocket, satellite, and AI company that’s valued at a premium to it and controlled by one person.

This is the end game. At least, it looks like Elon is running out of companies to fold together to hide underperformance.

#4411. Lunar’s new home DC fast charger puts your EV battery to work

Lunar Energy has unveiled a 25-kW home DC fast charger that will do more than just power up your car really fast. Paired with its next-generation home battery system, the Lunar Fast Charger will also let a compatible EV help keep the house running during an outage and potentially earn money by sending electricity back to the grid.

The new battery system will be available to customers in early 2027, with the charger rollout expected in mid-2027.

Lunar says its home DC fast charger can add roughly 100 miles of range in an hour at up to 25 kW. Actual results will depend on the vehicle and charging conditions.

This is a DC charger, according to Lunar’s product specifications. It connects directly to the DC side of the Lunar Battery, and Lunar says that setup avoids an electrical panel upgrade for the charger. The product page lists CCS and NACS connector support but doesn’t specify which cars will support bidirectional charging.

That distinction matters. Charging an EV and sending power back are separate capabilities, so buyers will need to check vehicle compatibility before relying on home backup.

With a compatible EV, Lunar says vehicle-to-home (V2H) charging could extend backup power through a multi-day outage. How long it lasts will depend on the car’s available battery capacity and what’s running in the house.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) payments will also depend on the availability of programs. They aren’t an automatic benefit of installing the charger.

The updated Lunar System has a 13.4 kW inverter and uses 5 kWh battery modules. A single tower holds 10–30 kWh, while towers installed side by side can provide up to 300 kWh.

Lunar is also expanding into small businesses, with pad-mounted configurations reaching 1 MWh. Businesses could use the batteries for backup and to reduce demand charges, or fees tied to their highest power draw.

The system can work with new solar using Lunar Maximizer panel optimizers, existing solar, or no solar at all. Lunar says assembly takes place in California, Georgia, Idaho, and Washington, with engineering and R&D in Mountain View, California.

Lunar AI uses electricity prices, weather forecasts, and a property’s energy use to decide when to charge batteries or supply power. Adding the EV gives it another battery to coordinate with rooftop solar and household battery storage.

The company reports that its California customers using Lunar AI saved an additional $338 on average last year compared with a standard battery operating mode.

Lunar’s Gridshare platform already manages more than 150,000 distributed energy devices worldwide. It groups those resources into virtual power plants (VPPs), allowing utilities and other energy providers to call on stored electricity when demand rises and offer customers incentives for participating. It currently operates VPPs in California, Hawaii, and Texas and is expanding in Utah, Nevada, and New Jersey. It also operates in Europe, the UK, and Japan.

Lunar hasn’t yet disclosed pricing or named compatible bidirectional EV models. Those are two important details homeowners will need before deciding whether this setup makes sense for their driveway.

#4410. Slate Is Selling A $30 'Screenless GPS' For Its Low-Tech Truck

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Slate has introduced a new "Screenless GPS" for its bare-bones EV pickup. It has zero boot time, no subscription fees, unlimited battery life, and absolutely zero chance of telling you to make a left turn into an active construction site since it, well, doesn't actually do turn-by-turn directions.

If you haven't caught on yet, it's a book: Rand McNally's 2027 Road Atlas, to be precise. On Thursday, Slate added the map to its online store for $30, calling it "the original navigation system." Slate said it's available in limited quantities.

The new product is clearly tongue-in-cheek and a bit of a stunt, but it also speaks to what Slate is trying to pull off. The startup is betting that people are fed up enough with complicated, modern cars to embrace a no-frills EV with unpainted composite body panels, manual windows, and no big infotainment screen. That, of course, means no built-in navigation either.

Obviously, few drivers actually want to use a physical map these days. Fortunately, the Slate will come with a phone mount, so owners can continue using their favorite mapping apps, like Google or Apple Maps. And hey, maybe that Slate-branded Atlas could come in handy in a pinch.

"When it comes to tech, we believe you should use the devices and solutions you already know and love," Slate said Thursday. "Not because we don't like tech, but because we believe you already have everything you need to get where you're going."

That minimalist mentality is what has kept the battery-powered truck under $25,000. You get an LFP battery, a bed, some wheels, and freedom from the complexities of the modern automobile. And if you really do want to add on some extras, they can be as analog as a map, or as digital as your phone. Or as involved as an SUV kit with extra seats and a roof.

It's a bold bet in an era when cars seem to only be getting more expensive and more packed with screens. We won't have to wait too long to see if the gamble pays off. Slate plans to deliver its first trucks later this year.

#4409. Our Long-Term Ram 1500 Taught Us to Love Hurricanes

Over 40,000 miles of towing, hauling, and road tripping, our six-cylinder Ram acted more like a BMW wearing Carhartt.

Our expectations for the Ram 1500 are well established. This being the third 1500 of the current generation we’ve put through a long-term test, the only real question mark was under the hood.

For 2025, Ram pulled the Hemi V-8 from the lineup. In its place came the Hurricane: a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six making 420 horsepower and 469 pound-feet of torque in its base form. Sure, that’s more power than the Hemi produced, but some buyers hold V-8-powered full-size trucks as a fundamental truth, right next to basic arithmetic and gravity. These folks would probably dismiss the Ram’s twin-turbo six outright. Their loss.

Over 40,000 miles, our Big Horn 4x4 model was a six-passenger, 5765-pound workhorse for all manner of tasks: towing trailers, swallowing luggage, devouring interstate miles, and hauling the kind of oversize objects people buy because they have access to a pickup, a credit card, and a Costco membership.

See all results for used 2025 Ram 1500 for sale near 94402

With the Hurricane, the Ram proved smooth, strong, and surprisingly sophisticated, like a BMW wearing Carhartt. We loved its power too. Our initial testing logged 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and the quarter-mile in 13.6 seconds at 100 mph. That’s serious pace for a crew-cab pickup on Falken Wildpeak all-terrain tires, and it was 1.3 seconds quicker to 60 mph than the 395-hp 5.7-liter V-8–powered 2019 Ram 1500 we ran through a 40,000-mile test. Our 2025 example repeated its 60-mph time at 40,000 miles, though its quarter-mile effort slipped a little to 13.8 seconds at 96 mph. Still, leave it in rear-drive mode, and the traction-control light will occasionally flicker during moderate freeway acceleration in the wet. That is not a complaint.

Indeed, driving the Ram 1500 leads to few complaints, which is why it’s been on our 10Best list eight times. The 1500, with its four-corner coil-spring suspension, rode with the calm authority that has long separated this truck from its rear-leaf-spring competitors, cruising and towing with the ease of a long-legged Clydesdale at a trot and making you wonder why other pickups don’t ride this well.

The Ram was a happy mile eater, as the optional 33.0-gallon fuel tank regularly showed more than 500 miles of indicated range after a fill-up. The cabin was a great place to while away the hours. Ram has been doing excellent truck interiors long enough that the surprise has worn off, but the usefulness remains. The front bench gave us seating for six and a healthy dose of nostalgia, the rear seat offered limo-like sprawl-out space, and the front armrest placed a hand naturally in line with the shifter and stereo controls.

Our most vocal complaints fell on the large mirrors from the Trailer-Tow Group package. They were fantastic when there was a trailer behind you and a nuisance when there wasn’t, blocking entire cars at roundabouts and requiring chicken-like head bobbing to see around them.

See all results for used 2025 Ram 1500 for sale near 94402

Worse, the mirrors fold and extend manually on this near-$70,000 truck (power-extending and folding mirrors are available). Also missing is passive entry, because Ram limited its availability for 2025 to Laramie and higher trims, and we didn’t notice when we ordered ours. Oops. We did go for the Big Horn Level 2 Equipment Group, which adds a 12.0-inch touchscreen, heated front seats, a heated steering wheel, dual-zone climate control, navigation, and a larger digital display in the instrument cluster. Keyless entry should be part of that package. Having to get the key fob out to unlock the doors would be acceptable on a contractor-spec truck. Or in the year 2015.

Remote start was present but inspired its own confusion. It would not operate with the fuel tank at a quarter full or below, which seems overly cautious when a quarter tank is over eight gallons and could get you halfway to Chicago from Ann Arbor. A considerable delay from when you double-tap the button to when the engine starts raised doubts that it had worked. This is especially charming on a winter day when your spouse is standing beside the truck holding a toddler who has entered the combat phase of development.

Fuel economy was the other great qualifier. We averaged 15 mpg; our long-term 2019 Ram V-8 managed 14. On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, the new Ram returned 18 mpg while the V-8 logged 17. A real-world 1-mpg improvement isn’t the efficiency promise we were told would justify ditching two cylinders. Instead, the Hurricane delivered improved acceleration, which is arguably a better bargain.

The last great frustration was our dealer’s service center and how often we visited it. Scheduled maintenance came at 10,000-mile intervals. Each appointment at Suburban Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Ann Arbor was more expensive than we expected. Examples included $60 for a cabin air filter that retails online for roughly half that and added services that aren’t in the owner’s manual.

High prices didn’t end at the service department either. A plastic clamp and a section of railing broke on our trifold tonneau cover, likely from one of us loading the bed with more enthusiasm than finesse. A replacement tonneau cost $2200 at the parts counter, which is curious considering it was a $550 factory option. We replaced the broken pieces instead, but even those bits cost $148. All in, our out-of-pocket maintenance costs amounted to $829.

The unscheduled visits were more troubling, because there were five of them. When the truck arrived, it couldn’t tow until we replaced the integrated trailer-control module, and that required a return visit once the part arrived. Around 18,000 miles, the forward-collision warning stopped working. At roughly 30,000, a wastegate actuator failed, throwing a check-engine light and effectively shutting off the turbochargers. Near the end, the infotainment system needed a dealer visit for an update. None of these problems stranded us or created a repair bill, but considered together, they made us wonder about reliability outside the warranty.

The Ram stayed beloved anyway, because the driving experience and utility outweighed the annoyances. Ram revived the Hemi for 2026. It’s as charming as ever and sounds amazing, and anyone claiming immunity to a V-8 pickup should have to explain themselves under oath. The smooth turbo six-cylinder is more efficient (slightly), powerful, and modern in ways you feel every time it comes onto the boost.

We entered this test wondering whether a six-cylinder Ram could make us forget the V-8. Forty thousand miles later, we remember it just fine. We just wouldn’t order one.

“The peaceful ride of a luxury car, the acceleration of a sports car, and the cornering ability of, well, a pickup.”—Tony Quiroga

“I drove five hours in a snowstorm. In 4WD Auto, the Ram 1500 handled the challenge with ease.” —Collin Morgan

“I find myself feeling at peace in the Ram.” —Caleb Miller

“I drove about 500 miles with the truck unloaded, then 500 miles pulling a side-by-side, and can say this just might be the perfect road-trip vehicle.”—Dave VanderWerp

“Nix the tow mirrors and add a proximity key, and you’ve got a practically perfect full-size truck.” —Greg Fink

“Despite creating forward-facing blind spots the size of Texas, the tow mirrors were great for seeing behind a trailer during a seven-hour trip.” —Jack Fitzgerald

“There is no better half-ton truck for a long-haul road trip.” —Eric Stafford

Our two regrets of our long-term Ram’s build are the lack of passive entry and the Dumbo towing mirrors. Ram now includes the former item on the Big Horn Level 2 Equipment Group, but ditching the latter means going without the helpful, but unnecessary, surround-view camera. So, scratching the mirrors but keeping everything else the same results in a 2027 price of $69,985. It might be the perfect non-luxury-spec pickup.

Thirty thousand miles in, associate news editor Caleb Miller offered perhaps the strangest compliment a pickup truck has ever received. "I find myself feeling at peace in the Ram," he wrote in the logbook.

At peace. In a pickup truck. That's either a testament to this truck's deeply soothing character or evidence that Miller should talk to someone. But he's not alone. Praise for the Ram has run throughout its logbook since the truck showed up. There's a steady stream of staffers angling for the keys each week.

So, it's a real shame that the truck can't stay out of the service department.

Managing testing editor David Beard started the Ram one morning on a road trip and climbed in to find the check-engine light glowing with the quiet menace of a "we need to talk" text. The truck seemed to be running fine, so Beard made the three-hour drive home. It was somewhere along I-75, as the Ram began downshifting on hills that had never previously required it, that he realized the Hurricane inline-six engine wasn't making full power. A scan tool confirmed his suspicion: a wastegate-actuator fault. The turbos had effectively clocked out.

The dealership unplugged the actuator, checked the wiring from the control module to the wastegate, found it all in order, and replaced the actuator. The fault cleared and hasn't returned. It's the sort of repair that is both reassuringly straightforward and philosophically loaded. Nobody who ever owned a factory Hemi V-8 has Googled "wastegate actuator." The Hemi just existed, doing its thing.

Elsewhere in the durability report, the trifold tonneau cover suffered a structural failure when both a plastic clamp and a piece of railing broke; the likely result of a load shifting in the bed or someone being less than delicate while loading it. The result: One morning on the freeway, the cover began performing a convincing impression of a sailboat. We removed it. An OEM replacement carries an MSRP of $2200 from Mopar. That's four times the $550 option price on our 2025 model's original window sticker, so we'll attempt to repair the broken clamp and rail piece first. Stay tuned.

These issues join a growing list. The Ram arrived needing its integrated trailer-control module replaced to fix an intermittent trailer-light issue that prevented us from towing. Later, a malfunctioning forward-collision system required a dealer visit to swap the long-range radar module. These aren't catastrophic on their own, and both were covered under warranty, but they add up to a truck that has required four unscheduled service visits in 30,000 miles.

What the Ram does between those visits, though, still makes the case.

Vehicle testing director Dave VanderWerp covered 500 miles unloaded and another 500 miles pulling a side-by-side. His verdict? "This may be the perfect road-trip vehicle," he wrote. "The air suspension is great for levelling out the load, and somehow it knows the trailer is 20 feet long and the blind-spot-monitoring system adjusts accordingly."

VanderWerp then noted with remarkable casualness that the truck was very stable while towing at 80 mph, and it got 10 mpg in the process. Hey, this is the U.S.A., and we have places to go.

He was less convinced by the Trailer Reverse Steering Control system, consisting of a knob on the dash that lets you steer the trailer while the truck handles the wheel. "Seems much easier and straightforward to just steer myself," he wrote, arguing that sometimes the best user interface is a steering wheel and a functioning human brain.

But for all its towing prowess and sophistication, we are baffled by the amnesia of the Tow mode button. If the truck is smart enough to detect a 20-foot trailer, it should be smart enough to remember you'd like to be in Tow mode when you restart the engine with the trailer still attached. Instead, it resets the drive mode every ignition cycle.

Fuel economy, meanwhile, has regressed. After climbing from 14 mpg at the introduction to 16 mpg at our 20,000-mile update, the average has fallen to 15 mpg. Towing—at 80 mph—will do that. The lifetime number appears to be settling around 15, which falls 4 mpg short of the EPA's 19-mpg combined rating. As a reminder, our 2019 V-8 Ram delivered 14 mpg across its entire test.

None of this has dimmed the enthusiasm. Miller is still at peace. The logbook is still full of praise (mirrors aside). And the sign-out sheet is still full of names. The Ram 1500 is the kind of truck that makes you overlook its flaws not because they're small but because everything else is that good. Whether that's a compliment or a warning depends on how you feel about those kinds of relationships.

Months in Fleet: 11 months Current Mileage: 35,410 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 15 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 490 milesService: $543 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0

Let the record show that after this 20,000-mile update we are enacting a strict ban on all complaints regarding the Ram 1500's side-view mirrors. They are massive. We get it.

Yet no matter where an entry in the Ram's logbook begins, the commentary inevitably careens toward those two opaque walls of plastic and glass that often eclipse the sun, the horizon, and occasionally, entire vehicles.

To wit, online production assistant Sarah Taylor was rattled after a four-way stop where the driver-side mirror successfully hid an entire sedan stopped to her left. "OMG, you can't see anything out the window," she said.

Other notes since our 10,000-mile update? "I'm short," wrote managing road test editor Becca Hackett. "I look like a chicken trying to move my head around to see around that new huge blind spot."

One writer described them as "forward-facing blind spots the size of Texas."

Another? "Dumbo ears." If the eyes are the windows to the soul, it seems the towing mirrors are the blast shields to reality.

Fortunately, even the skeptics concede that once you load up a trailer and escape the confines of parking lots and city streets, the Ram settles into its role as a supreme highway cruiser. Associate news editor Jack Fitzgerald gave a "shout out to the graphic on the screen that shows exactly how much angle your steering input gives while reversing a trailer." He also admitted that "the tow mirrors were mighty useful on a seven-hour drive pulling a trailer from northeast Wisconsin." Other staffers who tow more frequently have voiced similar mirror approval, if sheepishly.

It turns out judging the mirrors in a metro Detroit roundabout is like reviewing a deep-space telescope based on how well it works as a reading glass. Except you can't swap glasses because this telescope is effectively duct-taped to your face. Managing testing editor David Beard compared his experience entering a Cape Cod roundabout to a game of Russian roulette.

As we cross the halfway point of the test, small cracks begin to emerge in places other than the mirrors. We've noted a clunky 1-2 upshift and a lethargic response to downshift requests that can make city driving feel unpolished. An issue with the forward-collision system required a dealer visit to have the long-range radar module replaced (that repair was covered by the warranty). We've also caught the digital instrument cluster daydreaming: It displays a graphic of the pre-facelift Ram 1500 on multiple screens. After finishing a highway fuel-economy loop that returned 18 mpg (2 mpg better than our average thus far), road warrior Jacob Kurowicki said, "I couldn't wait to get out because of back pain."

Most other comments relating to the interior have been more kind. Technical editor Mike Sutton praised the existence of analog gauges in a world where almost everything's gone digital. Ditto for the front three-across seating, which brings back childhood memories—though we remain profoundly grateful that the nostalgia stops short of locating the fuel tank behind the seatback.

But because all roads lead back to the side mirrors, they have a throwback touch of their own: They fold manually. Shutting those barn doors means getting out and walking to both sides, which is acceptable on a base trim level, but an indignity at $68,320. Sort of how you still have to fish the key fob out of your pocket to unlock the thing.

Senior editor Greg Fink said it best: "Nix the tow mirrors, add a proximity key, and this is a near-perfect full-size truck."

Months in Fleet: 8 months Current Mileage: 23,570 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 16 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 520 milesService: $350 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0

The first 10,000 miles with a new vehicle are the exciting first dates before the mundane sets in. You're still gleefully memorizing the dashboard's contours, and the factory scent hasn't yet been fully vanquished by spilled coffee (or worse). With our long-term Ram 1500, this phase concluded with an exchange at our service department that felt less like a transaction and more like a scene from Burn After Reading.

It started with an innocent request for an oil change and a cabin air filter as part of the first service dictated by the Ram's oil-life monitor. The estimate returned with two surprises. The first was the cabin air filter itself, priced at a startling $60 (the part retails for roughly half that online). The second was $17 for something called Frigi-Fresh, a disinfectant for HVAC systems.

When questioned, our service advisor shrugged. Frigi-Fresh, he explained, auto-populates on the work order with every cabin air-filter replacement. By his logic, Frigi-Fresh is not an option but an inevitability.

Road warrior Jacob Kurowicki queried: "We have to tell you we don't want something that we don’t know we're going to get?"

"Look man, I just work here," the advisor said, providing the modern-day epitaph for personal responsibility.

A memo to those patronizing Suburban Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram of Ann Arbor: Declining unwanted extras requires telepathy.

The experience is the kind of thing that makes you want to change your own oil, even if it means remembering that the High-Output variant of the Hurricane engine requires 0W-40 synthetic versus the regular's 0W-20. At least the HO's special blend costs 171 percent less per ounce than Frigi-Fresh.

While it may not have the most desirable cylinder count, Ram's Hurricane twin-turbo straight-six is compelling, even if it feels as out of place in a Ram as a string quartet in a Waffle House. Stomp the gas and the soundtrack is less Woodward Avenue and more autobahn. It pulls with the confident, linear surge of something far more sophisticated.

The six-cylinder's impressive refinement carries through to the chassis and optional air springs, which testing director Dave VanderWerp called perfect for Michigan's annual Pothole Fiesta. Consider the Ram, then, a 5765-pound limo that shrugs off road blemishes with serene detachment, making it the king of long-distance hauls. You could transport a sleeping infant in the back across a railroad crossing and the most you'd worry about is the lingering scent of Frigi-Fresh.

VanderWerp also noted that the heated cloth seats get hotter than permitted by the lawyers at other automakers, who have probably calculated the precise temperature at which a human posterior bursts into litigation.

And then there's the mirrors. We have the optional trailer tow mirrors on our truck. They stick out nearly a foot on each side, stretching 102.3 inches tip to tip. That's 8.5 feet; any wider, and you'd want a pilot car. When towing, the mirrors provide an excellent IMAX-like view of your 24-foot enclosed trailer. The other 98 percent of the time, they stick out with the unearned confidence of a cryptocurrency enthusiast, requiring geometry in fast food drive-throughs and faith-based arithmetic in roundabouts. The tow mirrors are a wonderful solution to a problem we only occasionally have.

Just a little more than 10,000 miles in, and our Ram has already proven itself as a brilliant, comfortable, and quick long-hauler. It's a machine so thoroughly modern that it makes you forget all about the guttural appeal of two extra cylinders. That is, right up until you're confronted with the 15 mpg we've observed so far, one measly mpg more than our result from the 2019 V-8 Ram we tested a handful of years back. And clearly we aren't alone, judging by the V-8's quick return to the 2026 order sheet. Sometimes, progress is just a detour on the way back to where you started.

Months in Fleet: 5 months Current Mileage: 13,650 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 15 mpg Fuel Tank Size: 33.0 gal Observed Fuel Range: 490 milesService: $225 Normal Wear:$0 Repair: $0 Damage and Destruction: $0

What, another Ram? We're starting to feel like shepherds around here. This 2025 Ram 1500 Big Horn is the third Ram 1500 to undergo our 40,000-mile long-term test since 2019 (and sixth all-time), following a cushy 2019 Limited and an unhinged 2022 TRX. That's almost one every two years. So long as the Ram keeps collecting 10Best trophies (seven and counting), we'll keep inviting it back.

Speaking of sixes, the biggest change for this test is Ram's new six-cylinder engine. The flagship Hemi V-8? Gone from the Ram lineup entirely (for now). In its place sits the optional "Hurricane" twin-turbo 3.0-liter inline-six cylinder ($2695) that makes 420 horsepower and 469 pound-feet of torque. (The base engine remains a 305-hp 3.6-liter V-6.) We opted for a Big Horn trim with six seats because we liked that symmetry.

Between hauling race cars to track days, towing snowmobiles to Michigan's frigid Upper Peninsula, schlepping the family to weekend sports, and the endless parade of big-screen TVs from big box stores, this Ram won't be living easy. And our team's appetite for truck utility shows no signs of waning.

We opted for the 33.0-gallon fuel tank ($445), which should give us plenty of range for long hauls. We're eager to see if dropping two cylinders delivers better fuel economy than the 14 mpg we observed with the 395-hp 5.7-liter V-8–powered Ram 1500 we tested in 2019.

That truck was rated by the EPA at 19 mpg combined and so is this new Big Horn. What's the benefit of the six-cylinder then? So far, power. In our performance testing, this Big Horn reached 60 mph in 4.8 seconds and ran the quarter-mile in 13.6 at 100 mph, eclipsing that 2019 Ram by 1.3 seconds and 1.0 second.

We equipped this Ram for hauling with the Towing Technology Group ($595) and Trailer-Tow Group ($1345), which include everything from trailer-tire-pressure monitoring to side mirrors that are the size of elephant ears and boast power-adjusting convex glass. Throw in the 3.92 rear axle ($195), and we're cleared to tow 10,980 pounds and carry a 1350-pound payload.

The Big Horn Level 2 Equipment Group ($2770) brings the expected modern conveniences: a 12.0-inch infotainment touchscreen, heated front seats and steering wheel, dual-zone climate control, and so on. But in a head-scratching omission that would make a Porsche product specialist proud, passive keyless entry isn't included. Yes, our $68,320 truck requires manually hitting the unlock button on the key fob like it's 1995.

Excellent ride quality has been a longstanding attribute of the Ram 1500 thanks to its coil-spring rear suspension, which we upgraded with four-corner air springs ($1995). We can now also lower the truck to ease bed access while standing outside with the fob, which almost makes up for having to fish that fob out every time. Almost.

The Ram's interior has long set the standard for pickup luxury, though it was typically leather-lined higher-end trims earning that praise. We'll see if the excellence continues in our cloth-seat Big Horn. And we can have up to six critics weigh in on every mile.

#4408. BYD wins round one in Defender-copycat battle as JLR is told to destroy documents

BYD just got some good news in its Defender-copycat court battle with JLR. After JLR had BYD’s Netherlands offices raided and documents seized, a Dutch court has now handed BYD an early win, ordering JLR to destroy the documents or face a penalty.

After BYD opened orders for the Ti 7 in Europe and the UK in late July, many (including us at Electrek) compared it to the iconic Land Rover Defender, with its boxy, rugged (yet still elegant) SUV design.

BYD even described it as having “an unapologetically boxy profile” that delivers “the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”

In August, authorities on behalf of the British luxury automaker raided BYD’s offices in the Netherlands without prior warning and seized digital records.

On November 11, a Dutch court in The Hague ruled against JLR and ordered the company to destroy the seized documents, which included launch plans and other technical data, so they wouldn’t fall into anyone else’s hands.

JLR must destroy the documents within 24 hours of the ruling or face a fine of €50,000 ($55,000) for every hour it is delayed, with a maximum penalty of up to €500,000 ($553,000).

Within 24 hours of destroying it, JLR must also provide BYD with third-party confirmation that it has been destroyed. The court also rejected the British automaker’s request to pay a €500,000 ($553,000) fine.

According to Autoweek Netherlands, the ruling is based on the fact that JLR doesn’t need the documents, noting that the Ti 7 has not yet been sold in the European Union.

BYD won the ruling, and JLR is prohibited from taking any further legal action under the initial seizure order, but JLR has already begun summary proceedings over the infringement in Rotterdam and The Hague.

JLR claims that the Ti 7 SUV is a “slavish imitation” and infringes on the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender and that BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse-engineer some of its technology.

Before the raid, BYD claims it fully cooperated with JLR’s requests. BYD’s lawyers called the British automakers’ raid a “fishing expedition” and claimed that “too many files were seized.”

The Ti 7 is on sale starting at £47,995 ($64,000) in the UK, on the road. That’s over £20,000 ($26,500) less than the plug-in Defender 110, which starts at £71,840 ($95,500) in the UK.

It has a seven-seat arrangement, which BYD said was specifically designed for the European and UK markets.

As the first vehicle in the UK based on its DM-p (Dual Mode performance) powertrain, BYD said the Ti 7 “vastly exceeds the closest competition,” seemingly another jab at the Defender.

"JLR believes BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse engineer some of its technology"

Reverse engineering isn't illegal. Patent infringement is illegal.

Competition strip down each other's product all the time. As long as they don't use the "exact" same technology, it isn't a copy right issue.

The setup uses three electric motors and a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 402 hp (408 PS), enabling it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds.

The engine primarily powers a 35.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery, which provides a pure-electric WLTP driving range of up to 74 miles. In the city, it has an electric range of up to 102 miles.

Available exclusively in the UK in the flagship Excellence AWD trim, BYD claims that the Ti 7 offers “a level of equipment that exceeds anything that its rivals can offer at this price point.”

We should learn more about the BYD and JLR legal battle soon. Check back for updates, as this story is still ongoing.

#4407. A Record Number Of Uber Miles Are Happening In EVs

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Uber’s electrification efforts are looking better with every quarter, and this year’s third quarter has shown that the giant ride-hailing company is serious about lowering its fleet’s emissions. That said, Uber is also aware that, based on current trends, its 2030 goals “continue to be out of reach.”

Let’s focus on the good news first. Last quarter, Uber drivers across the globe completed a whopping 207.4 million rides in EVs, which boils down to over 26 EV trips on the ride-hailing platform every second, on average. Compared to the same period last year, the number of EV trips on the platform is 52% higher, but the big stats don’t end here.

In Europe, one in five Uber trips were done in an EV, while one in ten Americans and Canadians who took an Uber in Q3 wound up in an electric car. On average, there were 434,000 EV drivers active on Uber from July through September globally, up 52% from the same period last year,

When looking at the charts provided by the ride-hailing company, the difference between Europe and the U.S. and Canada is astonishing. Even from the start of the chart, in Q1 2021, Europe had a consistent lead when it comes to electrification, but the two North American countries were left in the dust starting in the third quarter of 2024. European drivers flocked to EVs, helped by various incentives and a boost in the charging infrastructure, while Americans' and Canadians’ uptake stayed relatively flat. For its part, Uber has offered cash bonuses to drivers who wanted to switch to an EV.

Despite the upward trends seen in the charts provided by Uber, it’s not all good news. The company has missed almost all of its sustainability targets for 2025 and is well on its way to missing its goals for the end of 2030 by a wide margin.

Just as the number of EVs on the ride-hailing platform has increased, plenty of drivers chose gas- or diesel-powered cars to make an extra buck on Uber. In the U.S. and Canada, every mile that a passenger traveled on Uber resulted in an average generation of 318 grams of carbon dioxide. That’s better than 2024’s 340 grams, but worse than the 306-gram average in 2023.

A similar story can be found in Europe, though the average vehicle emissions caused by Uber trips are vastly smaller than in the U.S. and Canada. Last year, 186 g of CO2 were put into the atmosphere in Europe for every mile traveled by a passenger on Uber. The figure is lower than in 2024 and 2023, but higher than the 183 g average in 2022.

The company said that the large gap between Europe and the U.S. and Canada can be linked to two factors. First, European drivers prefer EVs and hybrids more than American and Canadian drivers, but the more stringent fuel economy reporting standards in the U.S. also contribute to this discrepancy.

In 2025, the ride-hailing giant had wanted to see 100% of rides in London and Amsterdam be zero-emission. The outcome was just 41%. Furthermore, 50% of all mobility miles in seven European capitals were envisioned as being completed in electric vehicles, but the year ended with just 32%.

By the end of the decade, 100% of rides in Canada, Europe, and the U.S. should be zero-emission, but Uber is realistic and knows that it’s highly unlikely that it will finish 2030 with these numbers. Still, the company says it’s “deeply committed to this transition,” even though many levers are outside of its control.

#4405. sonnen’s new smart breakers help your home battery last longer

A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances. sonnen and SOLRITE Energy are putting that same principle to work for the grid, adding smart breakers that can temporarily switch off selected household loads while batteries help meet electricity demand.

The companies announced today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP). The setup combines sonnenHub with breakers that manage power-hungry equipment, both during outages and when the grid needs help.

The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.

A VPP connects home batteries into a network so they can work together as a larger energy resource. This addition gives SOLRITE another way to respond: in addition to controlling the batteries, it can reduce the amount of electricity that participating homes use.

sonnen and SOLRITE used the example of a pool pump, as it’s energy-intensive, nonessential, and runs for longer periods. When an event begins, ADAPT temporarily switches off the pool pump while the sonnen battery sends electricity to the grid.

With less battery power going toward the pump, more can flow to the grid. Across participating homes, that gives the VPP more flexibility than relying on battery dispatch alone.

Homeowners have to opt in to that grid participation, and ADAPT will switch off only pre-approved household loads. Joining the VPP program doesn’t give the operator blanket permission to turn off anything in the house.

“Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy.

The breakers also tackle a practical problem with home backup: Big appliances can drain a battery quickly, and the surge of power some equipment needs to start can overload a backup system just as an outage begins.

ADAPT coordinates the smart breakers with the sonnen battery to automatically switch off large loads during backup operation. When grid power returns, it restores them, so homeowners don’t have to go around resetting individual circuits.

That also gives homeowners more flexibility later. According to the companies, changing which smart-breaker-controlled loads are switched off during an outage doesn’t require rewiring those circuits.

The installation benefit matters, too. Some backup setups require electricians to move selected circuits into a separate panel. This system manages compatible circuits where their breakers already sit, which the companies say reduces installation complexity and inspection work.

Whole-home backup still has limits. Automatically managing large loads helps the available battery capacity go further; it doesn’t mean every appliance can run at once throughout an outage.

SOLRITE finances, builds, and owns residential solar-plus-storage projects through what it calls Virtual Power Plant Agreements, with no upfront cost to homeowners. It says it operates in Texas, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Illinois, with more markets planned.

#4404. Jensen Huang’s Departure from NVIDIA Sparks Hope of a Gaming Pivot

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

NVIDIA has announced that co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO whilst continuing as CFO, with Harvey Jones becoming the board’s first-ever chair. The announcement didn’t give a reason, although it obviously arrived after very public reports of extramarital affairs, one of them reportedly with a woman US intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. Neither NVIDIA nor Huang has confirmed the reporting, but investors reacted regardless, with shares falling as much as 14% at the open.

Masato Kumzawa addresses fan reactions to Grace Ashcroft's design and the impact of NVIDIA's DLSS 5 AI technology.

Ultimately, I’m not that interested in the gossip. What interests me far more is what happens to a company that has spent the last few years being defined by one man’s bet on AI, and whether that opens the door for the side of the business that first made NVIDIA a household name. For anyone who has tried to buy a graphics card recently, that is a rather important question.

Huang co-founded NVIDIA in 1993 and ran it for more than 33 years, with the move into AI being very much his decision. It has paid off enormously, because data centres now make up roughly 91.5% of the company’s revenue. The flip side is that nobody else has been quite as closely tied to that strategy, which makes for some interesting possibilities for NVIDIA’s future.

Kress has been CFO since 2013 and is a well-respected voice with the market, and eToro’s Josh Gilbert described her as a familiar and trusted presence, whilst adding that a company known for its technical edge might want an engineer in the chair. Analyst Dan Ives expects her stint as interim CEO to last around a year before NVIDIA looks outside. NVIDIA’s company structure is interesting in that it doesn’t make finding a solution any easier: Huang had more than 60 people reporting to him directly.

NVIDIA has no COO, and reports suggest there was no succession plan in place. The internal names analysts have put forward, such as Ian Buck, Bill Dally, Michael Kagan and Bryan Catanzaro, are largely AI and data centre figures, but none of them has been the face of the strategy in the way Huang was. Constellation Research’s Ray Wang pointed out that many of NVIDIA’s partnerships and investments came about because people trusted Jensen.

Which brings me to the hopium. NVIDIA started out making graphics cards for gamers, and CNBC has pointed out that those gamers helped keep the company afloat back in 1999 by buying the GeForce 256. These days they account for under 10% of revenue, and it shows: RTX 50-series production was reportedly cut by up to 40% earlier this year, the Super refresh was reportedly shelved, and the next generation has reportedly drifted towards 2028. Meanwhile, the RTX 5090 launched at $1,999 and third-party sellers have been asking far more than that ever since.

Nvidia DLSS 5 is officially supported in 2K27, but eager fans have found their own way to enable the software in a myriad of titles.

So it isn’t hard to see why some gamers are hoping the board promotes someone with roots on that side of the business. Jeff Fisher, SVP of GeForce, has been at NVIDIA since 1994, but it is obvious that Kress is probably the safer bet for investors. Jonah Alben, who has led GPU engineering since 2008, and co-founder Chris Malachowsky might also throw a hat into this race. It is however important to note that all of this is still very much speculation: nobody at NVIDIA has hinted at a gaming pivot, and whether that will happen with any likeliness will be heavily dependent on other factors.

Truth be told, I wouldn’t expect a new CEO to change much straight away, even one with a soft spot for gaming. The memory shortage squeezing GeForce is affecting the entire industry, with Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron reportedly prioritising AI customers for their high-bandwidth memory, and that won’t disappear because of who is sitting in the corner office.

Whoever takes over will also inherit a company that has just lost its founder and a fair amount of investor confidence, which tends to make boards cautious rather than adventurous. Even so, I’d quite like to see someone in charge who remembers where GeForce came from, and who has some sympathy for the people still trying to buy one. For now, Kress is running both the company and its finances whilst the search for a permanent CEO gets under way.

Between GTA 6's leaked pricing and the Steam Machine's $1,049 reveal, this week made one thing clear: gaming is getting expensive everywhere at once.

#4403. Tesla Just Killed Its Cheapest All-Wheel-Drive Model Y

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Getting an all-wheel-drive Tesla Model Y just got a lot more expensive after the American company removed the entry-level version of the crossover from its online configurator.

The Model Y All-Wheel Drive, which used to cost roughly $42,000, is nowhere to be found on the automaker’s website, which means the most affordable dual-motor Model Y is now the Premium AWD trim that starts at $51,630.

Introduced in February, the now-defunct Model Y AWD came hot on the heels of the budget-oriented Model 3 Standard and Model Y Standard that debuted in October 2025 as more affordable, rear-wheel-drive-only versions of the company’s best-selling EVs. When the bare-bones Model Y AWD was introduced, Tesla also dropped the “Standard” badge from its lineup, though the other trims are still called “Premium” and “Performance”.

Powered by the same battery as the single-motor Model Y RWD, the discontinued Model Y AWD had the shortest claimed range in the Model Y lineup, with an EPA-estimated 294 miles on a full charge—54 miles less than the most affordable rear-driven crossover in Tesla’s lineup currently.

With two electric motors providing motivation, the dropped Model Y AWD could sprint from zero to 60 miles per hour in 4.6 seconds, 2.2 seconds faster than its single-motor counterpart, despite weighing roughly 200 pounds more.

The cheapest Model Y in Tesla’s lineup remains the basic RWD version, which starts at $41,630. Compared to the better-equipped and more expensive trims, the entry-level crossover comes with redesigned front and rear lights, passive shock absorbers, a lower 225-kilowatt maximum charging power, fewer speakers for the audio system, and seats trimmed in vegan leather and cloth. There’s no FM radio, no rear screen, no ventilated seats, and only the front seats are heated. Furthermore, while the glass roof is still installed, the base trim has a headliner that covers it entirely.

The discontinuation of the Tesla Model Y All-Wheel Drive is just the latest casualty in the company’s quest to slim down its passenger-vehicle lineup. Earlier this year, the Model S and Model X were axed, and their production line has been ripped out of the factory to make room for robots. More recently, Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced that the Cybertruck would be retired next year. Until that happens, the only trim remaining is the top Cyberbeast, which starts at $109,990.

There are no plans to replace the Model S and Model X, and the Cybercab two-seater will take over the Cybertruck’s floor space.
